feat(text): distribute the gap between words for justify "full" (rich-justify-0cr.1) (#111)

`justify: "full"` was accepted everywhere and rendered as `left`: its branch
shared a body with left's, padding the line out to the canvas so it filled
without ever moving the words. It diverged from Python Rich on every block of
the pinned corpus.

The seam was the problem, not the arithmetic. `_justifyLine` is handed one
line, and `full` is the one mode that cannot be decided from one: the
reference leaves a paragraph's last line ragged and widens the gaps of every
line above it. Justification therefore moves up to the wrapped line —
`_justifyLines` — which is the unit Rich justifies too (`Text.wrap` calls
`Lines.justify` once per *logical* line, not once per render), and which
`Segment.divide` was already handing over whole. `_justifyLine` keeps the
three modes a line can answer alone, and its parameter drops `full` so the
type refuses what the function cannot do.

`_fillLine` reproduces the reference exactly: words split on a single space
with the blank a trailing separator leaves behind dropped, slack spread a cell
at a time from the rightmost gap leftwards, and each widened gap restyled from
the characters either side of it.

Verified by regenerating `text-justify.golden.txt` from Python Rich with
`full` in JUSTIFY — byte for byte, so the fixture stays the reference's own
output rather than a laundered copy of ours. Beyond it, a differential of
3,240 renders (27 texts x 24 widths x 5 modes) against Rich: `full` agrees
everywhere except two divergences that predate this change and belong to
other code — tab expansion is not tab-stop aligned, and a wide glyph at width
1 renders empty where Rich renders a space. Against HEAD the same harness
shows 574 changed renders, all of them `full` and none outside it.

Corpus gains one text. `uneven` ("a  bb cccc dddd") fills a line whose slack
will not divide evenly across three gaps, two of which are one space run the
author wrote; without it neither the remainder direction nor "a run of n
spaces is n gaps" was pinned, and mutating either passed the suite. Six
mutations — spread direction, even split, collapsing a space run, filling the
last line, keeping the trailing blank, and the gap style — now each fail.

The gap style is the one rule the fixture cannot see, being generated with
`no_color`, so it gets its own test with the reference command that produced
its expectations.

Table.expand and its skipped test stay open on rich-justify-0cr.3.

perf(text): fold spans into pieces instead of rescanning them (rich-text-6po) (#110)

`RichText._buildSegments` cut the text at every span edge and then asked, of
every piece, which of *all* the spans covered it. The pieces are cut by the
spans, so that charged `spans x pieces` — the square of the span count — and
anything styling densely reached it in ordinary use: a `ReprHighlighter` over a
large value, `highlightRegex` over a common character, `Pretty`'s indent guides.

Walk it span-first instead. A span covers a piece exactly when it covers the
piece's first character, because the pieces are cut at the span edges, so each
span owns one contiguous run of pieces and can be written into it once. Every
span edge is already a boundary, which makes the run's opening a map lookup
rather than a search.

Span-first also keeps the composition honest for free: `Style.add` is
order-dependent and the last writer wins, so the styles have to fold in
`_spans` order — which iterating `_spans` is, and which a position-ordered
sweep would have had to reconstruct.

Two dead guards went with it. Neither the empty-text early return nor the
empty-piece `continue` could fire: the boundaries come from a Set, so
consecutive ones always differ, and zero-length text produces no pieces at all.
A span covering nothing — empty, reversed, or past the text — still cuts the
text where its edges land, as before, and now folds into an empty run rather
than into a case.

Measured against e00600f8, same machine:

                                        before      after
  8,000 one-character spans             833.5ms      7.6ms
  4,000                                  62.7ms      4.8ms
  1,000                                  15.1ms      3.7ms
  Pretty nest(200), guides on          7081.0ms     82.8ms
  Pretty nest(100), guides on           758.1ms     25.5ms
  ReprHighlighter, 1,600 spans           61.2ms      4.0ms
  Pretty nest(1000), guides off         355.9ms    345.8ms

The last row is the control: guides off was never span-dense, so it is the row
that should not move, and it doesn't.

Output is unchanged. 2,798 renders — base styles, overlapping and identically
ranged spans in both orders, empty/reversed/out-of-range spans, all four
justifications with and without wrap, three highlighters, `Pretty` with guides
on and off, and the slice/divide/truncate paths — are byte-identical to
e00600f8.

The regression test counts span-bound reads rather than milliseconds, the way
`pretty.test.ts` counts getter reads: a wrong version still looks fast at any
input small enough to keep a test quick. It asserts the ratio between two sizes
so no constant has to stay true — 400 to 800 spans doubles the reads now and
quadrupled them before (241k -> 962k).

`pretty.test.ts`'s thousand-level render now runs at default options, with the
indent guides it had to disable to arrive. That is rich-pretty-51c's done-when,
which this unblocks.

perf(pretty): give the one-line probe its own traversal (rich-pretty-51c) (#109)

* perf(pretty): give the one-line probe its own traversal (rich-pretty-51c)

`_formatObject` asked each child what it looked like on one line by calling
the same renderer with a different `Frame`, and that renderer was free to
answer with a multi-line expansion. So the probe was a full render: every
child was formatted once to measure the parent's compact try and again to
place it, and a node at depth d was visited 2^d times.

  chain, depth 26         600ms -> 2.6ms
  wide tree, depth 12    6666ms -> 115ms
  formatting alone       exponential -> linear in node count
                         (4x the nodes, 4x the time: 17.5 / 70 / 213ms)

Split the two questions into two traversals. `_format` lays a value out at an
inset; `_oneLine` returns the single-line form or null. `Probe` carries no
`inset`, which is the point: a one-line form is the same string wherever it
lands, so the old `inset: 0` on a `Frame` is now a state nothing can write
down — and the `inset`/`level` collapse the ticket warns about has nothing
left to collapse.

What makes it linear is charging the budget before reading rather than after.
A budget checked only against finished text still walks the whole subtree to
produce text it throws away; charged first, every level costs at least its own
two brackets, so a probe descends at most budget/2 levels however deep the
data. Measured on a counting getter: 6 more levels now cost 6 more reads,
against 12,247 reads at depth 20 and 783,934 at depth 26 before.

Both traversals read one layout-free description of a container — `_shape` —
so the brackets, the elision marker, the empty case and the depth cap have one
home instead of four copies each. Two things fall out of that:

- `Map` and `Set` gain a one-line form. They had none, so a probe containing
  one came back already expanded and was accepted, because `cellLen` scores a
  newline as zero cells: `{ m: Map {` with the entry on its own line and the
  closing brace back at column 0. `fitOneLine` now names both halves of what
  fitting means. This is the only output change — a corpus of 22 shapes
  (long keys, maxDepth, maxLength, cycles, throwers, shared children,
  expandAll, narrow widths) is otherwise byte-identical to master.
- The depth cap and the empty case are answered from `.size` alone, before
  anything is enumerated. Reaching a position costs an iterator step, so a
  `Set` past the cap is no longer drained to print `Set {...}`.

docs/pretty.md said Map and Set are always expanded, which this changes, and
said their dropped entries carry no marker, which stopped being true when
PR #90 added `... +N` and a test for it.

The file grows 208 -> 292 lines of code: the second traversal was always
there, smuggled into the first as a field on a frame, and making it a type is
what costs the lines and buys the bound.

Not fixed here, filed as rich-text-6po: `RichText._buildSegments` rescans
every span per boundary region, so it is O(spans²). It reproduces with no
Pretty in the picture and hurts every dense highlighter. It is why the
thousand-level test passes `indentGuides: false` — guides are one span per
indent character — and it is the remaining gap to this ticket's done-when at
default options.

* perf(pretty): bound what a probe pulls by the line it is filling

A probe asked `_shape` for a container's positions before consulting its
budget, and the Map and Set arms reach a position through an iterator. So
probing `{ cache: hugeMap }` drained the whole map to discover the object
was too wide, then the layout drained it again to print it — and every
ancestor whose probe still had width to reach it drained it once more. A
5,000-entry map cost 10,000 pulls one level down and 20,000 at three.

This is the defect this branch already fixed one storey up. Charging the
brackets before reading bounds how many levels a probe descends; nothing
bounded how many positions each level pulls, so the per-level cost stayed
proportional to the collection.

`_shape` now takes the most positions its caller could ever use. Laying
out passes Infinity and still prints every entry. A probe passes what is
left of its line, which is already more positions than a fitting line can
hold: SEPARATOR charges two cells apiece, so a container with more
positions than its budget overruns whatever is inside it. Truncating past
that only ever feeds a join that returns null, which is why 216
shape/option combinations render byte-identical either way.

The bound is clamped at zero because a probe's budget goes negative once a
line is overrun, and `slice` reads a negative end as counting from the far
end — it would have kept all but the last few keys where `take` and
`Array.from` take none. One clamped derivation also replaces the three
separate `maxLength ?? …` spellings the arms carried.

docs(tables): remove the option rows the code does not back (rich-docs-c2w) (#108)

The page listed `safeBox`, `leading`, `collapsePadding` and `padEdge` as Table
options and `highlight` at both the table and column level. None is a member of
`TableOptions` or `ColumnOptions`, and nothing reads them. All six rows are gone.
None of the features was implemented to clear the row: each is filed on its own
merits in rich-table-60t, which carries the evidence that makes them look cheap
(`Box.getRow` already takes the `"mid"` level `leading` needs, `Segment.alignMiddle`
already does what a column `vertical` needs) together with the reason that is not a
reason to build them.

Auditing the rest of the page found more than the four the ticket named.

`ColumnOptions.vertical` was the worst of them, because it type-checked. It was
declared, stored on no field, carried by no copy, and read by nothing — the only one
of the set a caller could pass without a compiler error and get silence. The member
is deleted along with its row.

`style` is dead at both levels: `Table`'s constructor resolves and stores it and the
class never reads it again, and `Column`'s three style options survive `copy()`
without a single reader. `Table._renderRow` applies exactly one style to a finished
line — the table's `headerStyle`, `footerStyle` or a `rowStyles` entry — and never
the column's. Unlike `vertical` these are held rather than dropped, so they keep
their surface and get the treatment `expand` already had on this page: a row that
says it is accepted and not yet applied, plus a sentence naming what does style a
cell today. Wiring them is rich-table-jph.

The "Vertical alignment" section is deleted. It was fabricated end to end:
`src/renderables/align.ts` says in its own header that it aligns horizontally, and
`Alignment` is `"left" | "center" | "right"`.

Three snippets were repaired. The Table and Column constructor forms under "Adding
columns" never existed — both classes take a single options object. Both grid
snippets called `grid.addColumn({ justify: "right" })`, which lands that object in
`addColumn`'s header slot and discards the alignment the example depends on;
running it returns `justify: "left"`. The flagship snippet no longer teaches
`style: "dim"`, which does nothing.

`overflow` and `footer` were the inverse problem — real column options the page
never listed while its own prose leaned on `overflow`. Both now have rows.

`justify: "full"` is knowingly left alone; rich-justify-0cr.4 owns that row.

Two gaps this exposed are filed rather than fixed here: rich-render-nmy, because
`asciiOnly` is hardcoded false or omitted at all four `RenderOptions` construction
sites and so cannot be turned on by any consumer, which is where the `safeBox`
question really lives; and rich-docs-jqc, because no gate compiles a docs snippet,
which is why all four broken snippets above sat on a green suite.

docs(live): restore the cell markup addRow now parses (rich-table-5m9) (#107)

The basic-usage snippet was written as `addRow(job.name, "[green]done[/green]")`
on the assumption that cells parse markup, the way Python Rich does. They did
not — `addRow` built its `RichText` straight from the constructor and shipped
`[green]done[/green]` to the terminal with the tags intact — so rich-docs-site-13t.6
reduced the snippet to a plain "done" rather than describing a bug in prose.

The behaviour shipped with #96, which routed all five text positions through
`toCellText` as the single crossing. The snippet can go back to the form it was
written in.

Pinned the way `docs/tables.md`'s flagship row already is, with a test named for
the page: the crossing is covered, but a page-named test is what makes a
regression report the page that lies rather than only the function that broke.
This one puts the markup in the second cell of a two-column row, the position
the snippet actually uses. Confirmed red against a `toCellText` with its
`renderMarkup` call removed, where it reproduces the original bug exactly —
`| build | [green]done[/green] |`.

2336 pass, three-pass lint clean, `npm run docs:build` clean.

fix(box): leave an already-ASCII box alone under asciiOnly (rich-table-0gv) (#106)

`substitute({ asciiOnly: true })` answered `ASCII` for every box, including
the four that are already pure ASCII. A MARKDOWN table on a terminal without
unicode silently became a plus-and-pipe frame instead of the pipe-delimited
markdown it was chosen for; ASCII2 and ASCII_DOUBLE_HEAD were erased the same
way. The reference guards with "if options.ascii_only and not box.ascii".

Whether a box is drawable without unicode is derived from its grid at
construction, not declared per constant as the reference's `ascii=True` is.
A `Box` is wholly its grid, so the grid already answers this and a second
hand-written answer could disagree with it — and derivation reaches boxes no
constant speaks for: `safeSubstitute` builds a fresh `Box` from an edited
grid, and a flag on the shipped constants would say nothing about that one.
The predicate names exactly the four the reference constructs with
`ascii=True`, pinned by naming all nineteen in the test rather than asserting
the count.

This also fixes, with no change to table.ts, an asciiOnly + headerless
ASCII_DOUBLE_HEAD table. `Table.render` runs the two box swaps in the
reference's order, so `substitute` handing the box through unchanged leaves
`plainHeaded` a box it recognises: the frame is now ASCII2's crossed edge
("+---+---+") as Rich draws it, where replacing the box first left
`plainHeaded` holding ASCII and an uncrossed "+-------+".

Verified: six of the seven new assertions are red against the previous
box.ts. 2335 pass, three-pass lint and demo typecheck clean, golden files
unmoved.

fix(table): stamp the header and footer on assignment, not at the constructor (rich-table-n8a) (#105)

`toCellText` is the one crossing where caller content becomes table content,
and it makes three promises: markup is parsed, `end` is cleared because a cell
is a fragment rather than a line, and a `RichText` is copied so the caller no
longer owns the table's cell. `Column`'s constructor kept all three.

Nothing kept them after it. `Table.columns` hands out the live array and both
fields were plain and public, so an assignment landed unstamped in a slot every
reader below assumes the crossing has been through:

    const mine = new RichText("Foot");
    t.columns[0].footer = mine;   // no copy, no parse, `end` intact
    mine.append("MUTATED");       // and the table's footer changes with it

The invariant was established in a constructor and violable for the rest of the
object's life, which makes the stamp a convention the constructor happened to
follow rather than something the type proves.

Both fields are now accessor pairs whose setters route through `toCellText`, so
there is exactly one writer of the backing field in the program and the
constructor is one caller of the border rather than the one place it is true —
the same shape `Layout` already uses for `ratio` and `minimumSize`, which had
this bug for the same reason. `readonly` was the other candidate and is weaker
twice over: it is erased at runtime, and it would delete a capability the
reference has, where `Column` is a mutable dataclass. Assignment stays legal and
now parses markup too, because it crosses the same door construction does.

The setters take `undefined` rather than defaulting around it: absent and empty
are already the same header, and `toCellText` is where that mapping lives.

`copy()` stopped copying its own header and footer on the way into the
constructor — the crossing there copies a `RichText` already, and a second copy
is a second home for one rule. The existing "copy creates independent instance"
test grew the mutation assertion that makes that checkable.

The two `end` frames in the ticket do not reproduce, and the tests pin what is
observable instead: `_renderRow` justifies the cell to `cellWidth` before `end`
is appended and `adjustLineLength` crops it straight back off, so a header's or
footer's `end` never reaches the frame at any width or justification. The stamp
is asserted on the field; the copy and the markup parse are asserted through the
rendered output. Eight new tests, all red without this change.

2314 pass, `table-frames.golden.txt` unmoved and untouched, three-pass lint and
the demo typecheck clean.

fix(table): measure the cells the flags say are drawn (rich-table-8c8) (#104)

`_naturalWidth` sized a column against the wrong set of cells at both ends: it
seeded from the header unconditionally and never looked at `col.footer` at all.

The footer half lost data. A footer wider than everything above it got no column
wide enough to hold it, so a totals row — exactly the case where the footer is
the widest cell in its column — rendered as `…`. The header half wasted width:
a column was sized to header text `showHeader: false` had told the table not to
draw.

One rule, not two fixes. The reference's `_get_cells` appends the header cell
under `show_header` and the footer cell under `show_footer`, and both
`_measure_column` and `_render` iterate it — the measured cells ARE the drawn
cells. This port enumerated that set a second time inside the width path, and a
second enumeration is what let the two ends disagree with the draw path and with
each other.

`_columnCells` is now that enumeration, and the measuring loop lost its special
case with it: the header was a seed measured by a different expression than the
body cells, which is the same asymmetry that produced rich-table-n27 one
constructor line away. All three positions now flow through one `Math.max` over
one sequence, and membership is a flag rather than a guard.

Both reference frames pinned as tests, both red without this change. 2306 pass,
`table-frames.golden.txt` unmoved and untouched, three-pass lint and the demo
typecheck clean.

Filed while here, verified pre-existing by restoring master's table.ts and
re-probing: rich-table-3d3, a rowless table sizes to its header instead of
filling the offer, because `_naturalWidth`'s single number cannot say "no cells
to measure" distinctly from "measures zero" where Rich returns Measurement(1,1).

fix(table): let the flag alone decide the header and footer rows (rich-table-n27) (#103)

Rich draws these rows on `show_header` / `show_footer` and nothing else. This
port additionally required some column to have content, so a table that asked
for a row silently did not get one and nothing reported it. `showFooter: true`
with no footers anywhere drew no footer row at all; a table whose headers were
all blank lost two lines rather than one, because the guard sat above the head
separator as well as the row it was about.

The guards were the symptom. `Column.footer` was `RichText | undefined` where
Rich declares `footer: RenderableType = ""`, and that optional is what made
`some((c) => c.footer)` a well-typed, plausible-reading expression in the first
place. It also forced a `?? toCellText(undefined)` at the use site — an inland
guard compensating for the same missing constraint. Absent and empty are the
same footer, so `footer` is now built by the same one-liner as `header` one line
above it, and the two fields answer to the same question.

The asymmetry between those two constructor lines is what gave the bug away.
It also explains why the two footerless spellings disagreed with each other and
not only with the reference: `footer: ""` produced a truthy empty `RichText` and
unlocked the row, while no footer at all left it `undefined` and did not. The
drawing code was already correct and already matched the reference frame
character for character — only the guard deciding whether to reach it was wrong,
which is why the fix removes code rather than adding any.

Measured against Python Rich at width 20 across five shapes; all five now match
character for character. Four are pinned: the footer row with no footer, absent
and empty footers rendering identically, the blank-header row with its
separator, and `showHeader: false` still suppressing a header that has content —
that last one passes on the old code too and is there to catch over-correction,
not to pin the fix. The other three fail without it. `table-frames.golden.txt`
and the sentinel-grid test are unmoved, as is every other frame in the suite:
2304 pass, and no existing table has a blank header or asks for a footer row it
has no footers for, which is exactly why this survived.

Filed rich-table-76o while adjacent: `_naturalWidth` measures the header
unconditionally and never measures the footer, where the reference measures each
one exactly when its flag says it will be drawn. A long footer is ellipsized to
a single cell. Not caused or widened by this change — the footer rows it newly
draws are blank in every column, so there is nothing in them to truncate.

fix(markup): sort spans by start, so an inner colour survives (rich-markup-krk) (#102)

`markup.render` pushed a span when its tag closed, so the list came out
innermost-first, and `RichText` applies spans in list order with each one
adding over the last. The outer span landed last and covered the inner:
`[red]a[blue]b[/blue]c[/red]` printed all-red where Rich prints red/blue/red.
The inner run was not mis-ordered but gone.

Takes the reference's ordering rather than a re-derivation of it —
`sorted(spans[::-1], key=attrgetter("start"))` in `rich/markup.py`. The
reversal is the whole of the tie-break: two spans that both start at 0
(`[red][blue]x[/blue][/red]`) are separated by nothing else, and a stable sort
alone leaves the outer one winning.

That sort is defined against "the list is in closing order", and this port
broke that invariant in exactly one place: the auto-close walked the open
stack forwards where the reference pops it. The disagreement was invisible
while nothing sorted — it cancelled the missing sort, making `[red][blue]x`
the one nesting this port already got right — and would have become a
regression the moment the sort landed. It pops now, so all three closing
paths agree.

The three closing paths each wrote out the same "style string of an open tag"
expression, which is how they could drift on a property none of them was
about; one `openTagStyle` now answers it for all three and for the search
that matches `[/red on blue]` back to its opener.

Measured against Python Rich over 19 nesting shapes: 8 fixed, 0 regressed.
Two more moved decisively toward the reference and now differ only by
rich-color-7kv (SGR parameter order) and rich-link-jkh (OSC 8 `id`) — one of
them, `[link=x]a[link=y]b[/link]c[/link]`, previously collapsed the whole
string into a single link, silently discarding the nested one.

The golden gains `nested-colour`, `-tie` and `-unclosed`, regenerated from the
reference (the existing 23 cases reproduce byte for byte, so the fixture is a
pure addition). `nested-styles` stays as the additive arm — it reads correctly
under either order, which is why nothing caught this. The divergence test
written to fail on the day this was fixed is deleted, as it asked to be.

docs/markup.md said tags nest but never what an inner tag does to the run it
sits in; it now separates combining from overriding, with both examples
measured.

fix(markup): route every consumer through the one markup crossing (rich-markup-pcp) (#101)

* fix(markup): route every consumer through the one markup crossing (rich-markup-pcp)

`src/core/markup.ts` exported two functions that turn a markup string into a
`RichText`, and the four call sites in `src/` were split between them under the
same import alias:

    plugin-aware:  renderables/progress.ts, renderables/table.ts
    plain:         renderables/prompt.ts, core/console.ts  (`render as renderMarkup`)

The import line read identically at all four, so the difference was invisible at
every point of use. A tag registered on `globalMarkupRegistry` resolved in a
table cell and was silently eaten by `console.print` — the path almost every
consumer takes — printing the content unstyled with nothing reported.

Both plain sites now import `renderMarkup`. Measured, not assumed:
`console.print("say [shout]hello[/shout] now")` emits `say HELLO now\n`, and
`Prompt.ask` shows `pick ONE: `. `test/core/markup-grammar.golden.txt` passes
unchanged, which is PR #96's measurement — `renderMarkup` is a strict superset
that delegates on both early exits — confirmed end to end rather than re-derived.

`render` is now module-private: the ticket's open question, decided. Exporting
the inner layer is what made this bug representable, and unexported the drift is
a compile error rather than a rule to remember. Rendering *without* plugins stays
reachable as a value — `renderMarkup(s, { registry: new MarkupRegistry() })` —
instead of as a second function name. That also retires a second exported
`RenderOptions` that collided by name with the unrelated one in `core/protocol.ts`.

`examples/claude-sessions/.../_common.ts` carried the identical alias beneath a
JSDoc that already claimed `renderMarkup`; the two now agree. The plugin demo
gains the bare-string `console.print` path — the usage that was broken, and the
one every markup doc teaches.

`test/core/markup.test.ts` asserts the built-in dialect through the public
crossing with an explicit empty registry, so it no longer binds to an internal
function and cannot be perturbed by another suite's global registration.

* fix(markup): reject an overlapping plugin pair where it is detected

The top-level filter in `pairPluginTags` decided containment from where a pair
*opened* and nothing else. That one comparison read two different shapes as one:
a contained pair, which the recursion re-discovers when it renders the outer
pair's inner slice, and an overlapping pair, which has no contiguous region at
all. Both were skipped, so the overlapping pair's closing tag was orphaned into
the trailing slice and the built-in parser rejected it there — naming the wrong
tag, for the wrong reason.

Routing `console.print` through `renderMarkup` put that on the main path: with
two plugin tags registered, `[aa]x[bb]y[/aa]z[/bb]` printed `xyz` before (unknown
style names, non-strict nesting) and raised `MarkupError: Closing tag [/bb]
doesn't match any open tag` after.

Overlap stays rejected, because it is unrepresentable rather than unimplemented
— a handler receives `children` as one contiguous slice, so a region straddling
another pair's closing boundary has nothing to hand it. A style span may overlap
because it annotates; a plugin pair may not because it replaces. What changes is
that the rejection now happens where the shape is known and says so:

    Plugin tag [bb] overlaps [aa]: plugin tags must nest, because a handler
    receives one contiguous slice. Close [/bb] before [/aa].

Deliberately untouched: an inner plugin tag that never closes (`[aa]x[bb]y[/aa]`)
gets no entry in `pairs`, so it never reaches the overlap test and still renders.
The obvious alternative — rejecting whenever a closing tag's match is not the top
of the stack — would have broken it, which is why the test lives in the filter
rather than the walk. Pinned, along with sequential pairs and the built-in
dialect's non-strict nesting.

Found by review on PR #101.

fix(markup): take the reference's tag grammar, not a redrawing of it (rich-markup-sec) (#100)

* fix(markup): take the reference's tag grammar, not a redrawing of it (rich-markup-sec)

`TAG_RE` carried a hand-written character class where `rich/markup.py` has
`RE_TAGS`, and the two had drifted in both directions at once. It invented
uppercase, so `[INFO] starting up` was taken as an opening tag and printed as
` starting up` — silent text loss on every `Console.print`, since `markup.render`
is the path every string takes. And it omitted `@` plus every punctuation
character the reference admits, so `[a+b]` stayed literal where Rich styles it.

Replace the enumeration with the reference's own expression rather than a
re-derivation of it, so the two can be read side by side.

fix(text): word-wrap before the overflow method sees a line (rich-table-6uy.7) (#98)

* fix(text): word-wrap before the overflow method sees a line (rich-table-6uy.7)

`RichText.render` had no word-wrap step. `fold` chopped a line at fixed
cell multiples, `crop` and `ellipsis` cut the whole line, and a table cell
wider than its column was truncated where the reference wraps it. The
ticket's own case — a 10-cell column holding "aaaa bbbb cccc dddd" —
rendered `aaaa bbbb…` against the reference's two lines.

The fix restores the reference's order: divide the line at word
boundaries, fit each piece to the canvas, justify it. That order is what
makes the overflow method a last resort, so an unbreakable
`aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa` in the same column still ellipsizes; both arms are
pinned. It also deletes the branch it replaced — `noWrap`, a line that
already fits and a zero-cell canvas all reach the same pipeline as
values, and `_overflowLine`'s three-arm switch collapses into one crop
plus a marker.

`noWrap` becomes an unbounded budget rather than a skipped step, which is
what keeps soft-wrapped output and FlexStrip's too-wide fallback intact:
this port spells with one flag what Rich splits across `no_wrap` and
`overflow="ignore"`.

Table titles and captions were the same defect a second time — they were
rendered with `noWrap` and an explicit `crop`, so they were cut off at the
corner where the reference wraps them down the frame. Fixing that made
`_renderTitle`'s private justifier disagree with the one in `RichText`
over whether a wrap's trailing whitespace counts when centring, so the
alignment now happens in one place, matching `Lines.justify` on all four
modes.

Verified against Python Rich, not against this library:
`test/core/text-wrap.golden.txt` is 165 blocks of the reference's own
output over eleven texts, five widths and three overflow methods, with
the regeneration command in the test header. Deriving it turned up one
real divergence — Rich's `chop_cells` opens a blank line for a glyph
wider than the whole canvas and `chopCells` force-takes it — mirrored in
`foldWord` so the fixture stays regenerable.

The flagship docs example moves with it: at width 88 the Star Wars table
now matches the reference line for line, including the two-line Last Jedi
row and column widths the old block also had wrong.

Both existing modules shrank: text.ts 712 -> 703 code lines,
table.ts 517 -> 510.

* fix(text): resolve an unbounded width offer before justifying

`RichText.render` was the one renderable that never ran `withBoundedWidth`.
It hand-inlined the first half of it — a bare `cellCount`, which catches a
NaN width — and let an unbounded offer through, which was harmless while
nothing padded. This branch made `justify` pad, so `" ".repeat(Infinity)`
now threw `RangeError` from two separate sites: `adjustLineLength` on the
left/full arm, and the bare `repeat` on the centre/right arm. Guarding
either site would have left the other live, because the two crash for the
same reason in different code; the crossing at the front door is where the
reason lives, so that is what this restores.

Pins justification against Python Rich, which the branch changed and
nothing checked. All four of default, left, centre and right match the
reference block for block across 84 blocks — including the one this branch
set out to fix, where a wrap's trailing whitespace must not be counted when
centring. `full` does not match and is excluded from the fixture rather than
laundered into it: Rich distributes the gap between words and skips a
paragraph's last line, both of which need the whole render at once, and
`_justifyLine` is handed one line (rich-table-6uy.8).

Also drops a comment claiming `noWrap` carries Rich's `overflow="ignore"`.
`Console.print` maps that to `undefined` and `render` defaults it to `fold`,
which is what docs/console.md on this same branch already said.

* fix(table): let the frame outrank a title's own noWrap

A `RichText`'s own `noWrap` is OR-ed with the render option, so it cannot be
outranked by the options the table hands it. `_renderTitle` already cleared
`justify` for that reason, and the crop that used to bound the title is gone
now that titles wrap down the frame — so a caller who set `noWrap` on their
title got a line at its natural width, 49 cells out of a 20-cell table.

`overflow` stays the caller's. `noWrap` decides whether the line is bounded
at all and the frame is that bound; overflow only decides how a line meets an
edge it cannot move, and every method cuts within the budget. Clearing all
three is the cheap fix and it overrules a caller for no invariant's sake, so
there is a test standing on that distinction as well as on the frame.

* fix(text): measure a line's hanging whitespace from its text, not its segments

Where a line ends is a fact about its characters, but `hangingWhitespace`
asked its segments: it walked backward and stopped at the first segment not
ending in whitespace. An empty segment looks exactly like that to a regex
anchored at the end, and cropping a line to its budget leaves one behind — so
a styled line that had been cropped reported zero hanging whitespace and was
centred as though its content ran to the edge. A span landing anywhere inside
a wrap's trailing spaces silently un-centred the line that wrap closed, which
is a table cell with markup in it, centred.

Asking the line's text instead makes segmentation-independence hold by
construction rather than by walking carefully, and the walk goes away.

Pinned as a property, because segmentation is invisible from the outside and
was therefore free to matter: a span carries no cells, so a styled line must
place exactly where its plain twin places, and the plain twin is already
pinned to Python Rich by the fixture. Over the corpus, every width, every
mode, and a span at every offset — the only way to land one inside each run
of a wrap's whitespace. It failed on 24 of those before this commit.

* docs(console): describe what each overflow mode does, not what this call does

The three inline comments said this example cropped and ellipsized a word,
and the paragraph directly beneath said ordinary words wrap identically under
all three — which is what the code does, and what makes the comments the copy
that lies. `long` has no word wider than the line, so none of the four calls
cuts anything.

Python Rich substitutes the box itself when a table has no header — five of
the nineteen constants map to a plainer kin, the default HEAVY_HEAD among
them — and this port did not, so `showHeader: false` drew heavy header glyphs
on the top border of an otherwise light frame.

`Box.plainHeaded()` stands beside `substitute()` rather than joining its
options bag: one asks what the platform can draw, the other what the table
contains, and nothing correlates them.

The relation is keyed on the grid rather than on object identity as the
reference's dict is. A Box is wholly determined by its grid, so two boxes
carrying one grid must answer alike — and `safeSubstitute` already builds such
a box, a fresh instance with an unchanged grid, which identity keying would
have silently failed to substitute.

Also collapses the asciiOnly ternary at the callsite: `substitute` already
returns the receiver when the flag is off, so the outer branch was a second
place deciding one thing.

Pinned by the `no-header-no-footer` configuration added to the golden frame

fix(table): parse markup at the one crossing that makes cell text (rich-table-6uy.5) (#96)

* fix(table): parse markup at the one crossing that makes cell text (rich-table-6uy.5)

`addRow("[red]Solo[/red]: A Star Wars Story")` put the tags on the terminal.
The cause was not one missing parse but five separate ones: cells, headers,
footers, the title and the caption each built their own `RichText` straight
from the constructor, which by design does not parse markup. One rule, five
homes, absent from all five.

So the fix is a consolidation rather than five edits. `toCellText` is now the
single crossing every one of those positions goes through, and markup parsing
lives there once. Parsing is unconditional because that is what the reference
does — Rich's `Console.__init__` declares `markup: bool = True` and all five
positions reach the wire through `Console.render_str` — not because it was the
smaller branch. `toRenderable` loses its `instanceof RichText` arm: `RichText`
implements `Renderable`, so it already leaves through the renderable arm
untouched.

Two further defects surfaced, and both had to be fixed for the parse to mean
anything:

- `_renderTitle` rendered `text.plain`, reading the characters and dropping
  every span attached to them. Parsing without this would have been strictly
  worse than the bug: the tags would vanish and the colour would silently never
  appear. It now renders the content's own segments over the table's title
  style as the base, which is what the reference emits — `\e[3;31m` for a
  `[red]` title in an italic table title, italic and red rather than either
  one. The crop/pad fork went with it; `adjustLineLength` handles both by value.
- `_naturalWidth` measured the raw cell value, so a column sized itself to
  `[red]Solo[/red]` — fifteen cells for four cells of text. Measurement now
  asks the same crossing that renders it what the text is.

Verified against Python Rich itself, not against reasoning about it. The
docs/tables.md flagship example rendered at width 88 now matches the reference
character for character on six of seven lines, including both markup-bearing
rows. The seventh is a wrapping difference with no markup in it, reproduced
with none anywhere and filed as rich-table-6uy.7.

Each of the three gates was proven to go red, in isolation: dropping the parse
fails all six markup tests; flattening the title back to `.plain` fails exactly
Title and Caption; measuring the raw value again fails exactly the width test.

.4's golden fixture is untouched, as its own comment predicted — its cells are
plain digits precisely so this change could not move a frame in it.

* fix(table): stamp each cell once, and render titles the reference's way

Four defects the review surfaced, three of which this branch introduced.

Cells were converted twice per render — `_naturalWidth` and `_renderRow` each
resolved the raw value independently, which is two authorities on what a cell
is. They disagreed: a `Panel` stringifies to `[object Object]`, which the tag
pattern matches whole, so markup-parsing it in the sizing path returned empty
text and measured the column as zero. `addRow` now resolves each cell through
`toRenderable` once and stores `Renderable[]`, so both consumers read one
stamped value and re-parsing is unrepresentable rather than merely avoided.
Measured on a 500x8 table: 15.12 ms/render back to 10.52, against a pre-branch
baseline of 10.39. The cost is that `MarkupError` now surfaces at `addRow`
rather than lazily at render — a stated divergence from the reference, taken
because the error still surfaces with the same message and now points at the
call holding the bad string.

Sizing a cell that draws itself still stringifies rather than measures it, so a
`Panel` contributes a wrong non-zero width. That gap is pre-existing and stays:
`_columnDemands` carries no `RenderOptions`, so `Measurement.get` is not
reachable from there.

`_renderTitle` took only the first line, so a title carrying a newline lost
everything after it silently. The reference renders every line, verified by
running it — `"Line one\nLine two"` now emits both, centered, matching the
reference character for character. It also emitted a blank line for `title: ""`
where the reference emits none; the loop disposes of that too.

`titleJustify` was not the owner of its own alignment. A `RichText` carrying its
own `justify` pads itself to the full width inside `render`, collapsing the gap
and silently outvoting the table's option. The title now renders from a copy
with `justify` cleared.

Not fixed here, filed as rich-markup-sec: this port's tag grammar accepts
`[A-Z]` where the reference's accepts only `[a-z#/@]`, so `[INFO]` is eaten as
a tag here and printed literally there. That is a `core/markup` defect reaching
every `Console.print`, pre-existing and merely made reachable from a table cell
by this branch. Narrowing the class locally passes all 2259 tests unchanged,
which is the finding rather than the fix — the grammar is unpinned, and it
deserves the reference audit rich-table-6uy.3 gave the box data.

* fix(table): leave no phantom column when a cell's markup is malformed

Parsing at the border gave `addRow` a way to throw that it did not have
before, and the column auto-create loop ran ahead of the parse — so
`addRow("ok", "[/bad]")` on a one-column table raised `MarkupError` with a
second, empty column already committed. A caller that caught the error and
retried with valid data inherited the phantom.

Resolving the cells before the loop makes `addRow` all-or-nothing. The
operations are unchanged and still all run; only their order moved, so there
is no rollback path and no try/catch to keep correct.

The eager throw is a deliberate divergence — Rich stores the raw string and
raises the same `MarkupError` lazily at print time — so both halves are now
pinned: that `addRow("[/bad]")` throws where this port parses, and that the
failed call leaves the column list untouched. Each was proven to fail by an
isolated revert.

* fix(table): consult the plugin registry at the cell crossing

`core/markup.ts` exports two functions that turn markup into `RichText`, and
this file imported the plain `render` under the name `renderMarkup` — as
`console.ts` and `prompt.ts` still do. A tag registered on
`globalMarkupRegistry`, which `examples/rich-markup-plugins` does, therefore
degraded silently inside every table cell, header, footer, title and caption:
tag consumed, content unstyled, nothing reported.

The real `renderMarkup` is a strict superset. Both of its early exits — no `[`
in the string, and zero paired plugin tags — delegate to `render` with the same
base style and the same emoji default. Output was verified identical across
eleven markup shapes, malformed input raises the same `MarkupError`, and a
500x8 table showed no regression (plain 36.8ms -> 35.2ms, `[red]v[/red]`
57.4ms -> 53.6ms, median of ten runs). So this costs nothing a caller who
registers nothing can observe.

No registry threaded through `TableOptions`: that would be a mode with no
reference behaviour to define, and the global registry is the one `progress.ts`
already reads.

`toCellText`'s comment said those five positions reach the wire through
`Console.render_str`, meaning Rich's; it read as this port's `console.ts`. It
names Rich now.

The remaining console.ts/prompt.ts split is filed as rich-markup-pcp.

* test(table): pin the eager markup throw at every position that carries it

Parsing at the border moved the `MarkupError` from render time to the call that
supplies the string, and only the cell position was held still. The other four
convert just as eagerly — `Column`'s constructor for header and footer,
`Table`'s for title and caption — so a constructor that could not throw before
this branch can now throw at four sites with nothing pinning it.

Checked against the reference per position: Rich raises the same error from all
five, at print time. The divergence is uniformly when, never whether. The first
probe of that claim reported "no throw" for a title, because a table with no
columns renders no title and so never parsed it; a table with a row present
throws for every position.

One `it.each` rather than a test per site, matching the positional test a screen
above it and its stated reason — one rule with five call sites is one assertion
driven by five values. The single-position test it replaces is gone, so five
positions are now covered by fewer bodies than one had. Reverting any one
position to an unparsed `RichText` turns exactly that row red and no other.

No atomicity test for `addColumn`: `new Column(...)` already throws before the
push, so there is no defect there to pin.

* fix(table): clear end on a caller's RichText, not just on parsed markup

`title?: string | RichText` documents two input shapes and `toCellText` stamped
only one of them: the `instanceof RichText` early return handed the object back
untouched, so a `RichText` carrying its default `end` of "\n" kept it. An empty
one then drew a full-width blank line above the frame — the same stray line this
branch already removed for `title: ""`, still reachable through the other half
of the union, and at the bottom of the frame for `caption`.

The reference emits no line for either shape, so this was a divergence rather
than a preference.

The hole was the early return itself, not a step it forgot. Clearing `end` is an
operation every path owes; the input shape decides only how the `RichText` is
obtained. One branch now picks between `copy()` and a parse, and the stamp runs
after it unconditionally. The copy is what keeps the clear from reaching back
into the caller's object, and it carries style, justify, overflow, tabSize,
noWrap and the spans, so a title's own justify still arrives for `titleJustify`
to outrank.

`text.ts` is left alone deliberately. Its empty-text branch yields `end`
unguarded where the non-empty branch suppresses a bare "\n", which looks like
the deeper cause but is what makes `console.print(new RichText(""))` emit a
blank line at all. `end = ""` is how a caller says "fragment, not line", and the
table's crossing is where that already gets said.

The empty-content test now runs over both shapes in both positions, and compares
the whole frame: it read only the first line before, which is why the caption
half could not have been caught. Reverting the early return turns exactly the
two RichText rows red.

* fix(table): stop re-stamping a footer that was stamped at its column

Giving `toCellText` a `copy()` arm in f3cf43df turned the footer row's
`toCellText(c.footer)` from a pass-through into an allocation per column per
render — `c.footer` is already a resolved `RichText`, stamped once in the
`Column` constructor, so the copy bought nothing. The header line directly above
reuses its stored instance, and the two had no reason to differ.

Measured on a 500x8 table with a footer on every column, built once and
re-rendered: 4.28ms -> 4.16ms, median of 20 passes after 3 warmups. Modest, and
bounded by column count rather than row count; the consistency was the larger
half.

The absent case routes back through `toCellText` rather than spelling
`new RichText("", { end: "" })` at this site, so the rule that table content
carries no line ending stays at the crossing that owns it. It is also what the
data rows a few lines up already do for a missing cell.

A mixed table — one column with a footer, one without — was reachable through
no test. It is pinned now against the reference, character for character.
Sabotaging the absent arm's content reddens that test and only that test;
dropping the cell entirely reddens nothing, because `_renderRow` pads a short
list, so the test's comment claims the content and not the padding.

fix(box): declare each box style as the reference's own 8x4 grid (rich-table-6uy.3) (#94)

* fix(box): declare each box style as the reference's own 8x4 grid (rich-table-6uy.3)

A `BoxChars` carried five of the reference's eight grid lines. The three it
dropped are the row separator, the footer separator and the footer content row,
so a table with `showLines` or a footer drew the head-to-body glyphs where Rich
draws `├───┼───┤`, and no data edit could have fixed it — the type had nowhere
to put them.

Seven of the nineteen constants were also wrong on fields that did exist:
ASCII's top and bottom dividers, and the whole MINIMAL and SIMPLE families.

Both defects have one cause. The eighteen named fields were a second,
differently-shaped map of a territory the reference publishes as an 8x4
character grid, and every constant was a hand transcription into that shape —
including a name collision that inverts a box if read literally, since the
field named `mid` held the reference's line 3 while the reference's own `mid_*`
is line 4. So the fix is to stop transcribing: a `Box` is now built from the
grid itself, which can be diffed against `rich/box.py` character for character,
and the row glyphs are reachable only by what a row *is* (`getRow`,
`getContentChars`) rather than by a name that can be matched to the wrong line.

The nineteen constants were generated from the reference, not retyped. Frames
verified by rendering every one of them as a table with a header, two body rows,
row separators and a footer, and diffing all nine lines against expectations
computed from `rich/box.py`: 19/19 match, and corrupting one grid line makes the
diff red on exactly that row.

`Table` needed no edit — the level already crossed as a value, which is the seam
.1 and .2 left open for this. `Panel` reads `box.top`/`box.bottom` as records now
and takes its body verticals from `getContentChars("row")`.

The grid also carries `mid` as the reference means it: a blank spacer holding the
body verticals, not a rule.

611 lines to 435, while tripling the data each constant carries.

The constructor checked that a row held four characters. That is half the

line that caused it.

Both legs are now required and both are pinned by a test that fails when either
is removed: four characters, because getEdge indexes the four positions, and
four cells, because that is what is drawn. The previous test claimed to prove
the character count was not a UTF-16 count and could not — its input was all
BMP, so both readings agreed and reverting the check left it green.

It said all thirty-two characters were distinct and that swapping any two
would turn the test red. Thirty are distinct; a content row's fill column is a

feat(color): ramp — a number becomes a colour over ordered stops, in OKLCH (#92)

* feat(color): ramp — a number becomes a colour over ordered stops, in OKLCH

`ColorRamp` (src/themes/ramp.ts) maps a measurement onto ordered colour
stops: `linear` interpolates between adjacent stops in OKLCH, `step` holds
each stop until the next — a threshold cascade (`≥ 50 warning, ≥ 80 error`)
written as data. One class, the easing a value. Values clamp at both ends
and a value on a stop returns that stop's colour byte for byte, so a step
ramp never paints a colour the author did not write.

`Oklch.mix` is the interpolation: shorter hue arc, and an achromatic
endpoint adopts the other's hue (CSS Color 4's powerless rule), using the
same ACHROMATIC_EPS `fromRgba` pins hue by.

The template binding `ramp <value> <easing> <position> <color> …` sits
beside `color` in `paletteFuncs`: stops are colour references resolved
through `resolveColorRef` against the live palette on every evaluation, so
a ramp over palette names recolours with the theme. The argument list is
one float/string cycle end to end, typed by the engine's `alternating`
gate; the pairing and the references are parsed once in `colorStops`.

Docs, both colour demos, and tests cover the module, the OKLCH mix, and
the binding.

* docs(ramp): the ramp example builds an engine that has ramp; stale reader lists stop naming readers

The template-bindings doc's ramp example used createRichTextEngine(), which
wires richTextFuncs() alone — ramp is a palette function (its stops may be
palette names) and lives in paletteFuncs, so the pasted snippet threw at
evaluation. It now builds the engine the way the doc's own palette section
does, with both maps.

The ACHROMATIC_EPS comment enumerated its readers and went stale the moment
mix() became a third; it now states the invariant without a list, so no
reader can stale it again. The studio's ramp import label pointed at
section 6; the demo lives in section 5.

* fix(oklch): one achromatic rule for every Oklch producer; mix refuses t outside [0, 1]; ramp names a missing value

`mix` pinned no hue on its result, so `gray.mix(blue, 0)` was a zero-chroma
colour wearing blue's hue — a gray `fromRgba` would never produce, breaking
"achromatic means h = 0". The pin is now ONE function, `hueOf(c, h)` beside
`ACHROMATIC_EPS`, applied by `fromRgba`, `applyKey` and `mix` to their
results (the two inline pins are gone); the constructor still passes
intermediates through by contract. The lerp moves to the endpoint-exact
`a*(1-t) + b*t` form, so t = 1 lands on `toward` bit-for-bit on every axis.

`mix` is interpolation, not extrapolation: t outside [0, 1] (NaN included)
is a RangeError. `ColorRamp.at` already returns stop colours before mix
sees an out-of-range t.

`{{ ramp }}` with no arguments reached the body and threw the misleading
"needs an easing after the value"; one arity check over the whole argument
list now names what is missing and how many arrived.

The two module comments name `color` AND `ramp` as the palette-dependent
functions.

* docs(template-bindings): richTextFuncs' docstring names both theme-bound functions, color and ramp

* test(template-bindings): the palette-bound inventory is color AND ramp — comments and the bare-engine assertion say so

* fix(oklch): mix lands on each endpoint's hue bit-for-bit — unwrap the shorter arc by subtraction, then the same endpoint-exact lerp every axis uses

Hue took `(fromH + dh * t) % 360`, which at t = 1 is an addition of two
independently rounded values and reconstructs `toward.h` only by luck.
Now the larger endpoint of an arc wider than half a turn is taken a turn
down — `x - 360` for x ≥ 180 is exact by Sterbenz — and hue goes through
the same `lerp` as l/c/alpha; the final wrap adds 360 back to an exact
`x - 360`, whose real sum is representable, so it too is exact. Pinned
over a 6×6 grid of hue pairs at t = 0 and t = 1.

`wrapHue` is the one spelling of hue-into-[0, 360) and replaces the three
inline wraps in fromRgba, applyKey and mix.

fix(console): let print say what a value is, instead of nothing (rich-console-93r) (#90)

* fix(console): let print say what a value is, instead of nothing (rich-console-93r)

`console.print({ a: 1 })` emitted a blank line. Every argument that was not
already a renderable went through `String()`, which for an object yields
`[object Object]` — text the markup parser then read as a style tag and
consumed whole, leaving nothing at all.

`print` now sorts each argument into three arms, and they are the whole domain:
a renderable draws itself; a string is the only kind of argument that can
contain markup, so it is the only kind the markup dialect is applied to;
everything else is data, formatted by `Pretty`. Running a markup parser over
`String(42)` only ever worked by accident, and that accident is gone.

`Pretty` had to become correct first. It rendered a `Date`, an `Error`, and a
`RegExp` as `{}`, because `Object.keys` on any of them is empty — so routing
objects to it would have traded one silent information loss for another. It now
asks whether a value carries its own string form: a `toString` other than
`Object.prototype`'s means the value answers the display question itself, and
inheriting the default means the keys are all the information there is. Both
clauses of that predicate are load-bearing — the second makes
`Object.create(null)`, which has no `toString` at all, reflect rather than throw.
`print` used to throw a TypeError on such a value.

`Pretty` moves from `renderables/` to `core/`. Reaching it from `console.ts`
would have been a third sanctioned upward edge out of `core/`, and CLAUDE.md
says in the imperative that a third edge is the signal to reconsider the seam
rather than append to the list. Reconsidered: `Pretty` composes no other
renderable — the trait every other file in `renderables/` shares — its imports
are core primitives only, and its job is `markup.ts`'s and `emoji.ts`'s job of
turning foreign input into `RichText`. Implementing `Renderable` was never the
criterion for that directory; `RichText` implements it too. The mis-cut was
`Pretty` living above core, so the edge is deleted rather than sanctioned.

One deliberate behavior change beyond the bug: a trailing options object is
recognised only when something precedes it. `print({ style: "..." })` now prints
the object instead of nothing, and no content is lost — options configure the
rendering of content, so a call with options and no content had nothing to
render either way.

The dead `item instanceof RichText` arm is deleted; `isRenderable` caught it
first, so it was unreachable.

Docs: `introduction.md` and `console.md` asserted this behavior and were false;
`pretty.md` had been corrected to the broken behavior and is now false in the
other direction. All three now match, against captured output. `console.md`'s
`log()` section loses the bare-timestamp case and keeps the `{ end: ... }` trap,
which is real.

* fix(pretty): carry the caller's highlighter, and survive the data it is handed

Routing `print`'s data arguments through `Pretty` handed three things to a
formatter that was only ever reached deliberately before, and it was not ready
for any of them.

`highlight` and a custom `highlighter` are console-wide settings and stopped
reaching data arguments: `Pretty` held a module-level `ReprHighlighter` and used
it unconditionally, so `print(42, { highlight: false })` stayed coloured and a
`Console` built with a custom highlighter silently lost it for every non-string
value. `PrettyOptions` now takes `highlighter`, defaulting to the same
`ReprHighlighter` so a standalone `new Pretty(x)` is unchanged, and `print`
passes the console's — or `NullHighlighter`, so the disabled case is an identity
operation rather than a skipped call.

Self-referential data crashed the caller. `_format` recursed forever and threw
`RangeError`, where the `String()` it replaced merely returned an unhelpful
line. The traversal now carries the objects open between the root and the
current node, joined on the way down and left on the way back up, and prints
`[Circular]` on re-entry. The leave-on-exit is the whole design: a set that only
grew would call a shared child — one object reached twice through sibling
paths — circular the second time, and both cases are tested because neither
pins that alone.

Typed arrays lost their structure. `Int8Array` carries a `toString` distinct
from `Object.prototype`'s, so the self-description arm claimed it and answered a
bare `1,2,3` — no brackets, nothing for the highlighter to colour per element,
and indistinguishable from the string. They now reach the arm that formats
sequences, above self-description for the same reason `Array` sits there.

Also drops the `[LAW:parse-dont-validate]` citation on `describesItself`. The
token is canonical, but the citation was inapt: that law is about a check
returning a type that could not have existed before it ran, and `describesItself`
returns a boolean — the validator shape the law contrasts against.

* fix(pretty): bound what print formats, and stop one number meaning two things

UNVERIFIED: tsc --noEmit passes; the vitest run was cut off by a context limit before completing. Run 'npm run lint && npm test' first.

Round-2 review findings. print now formats arbitrary data, reaching two Pretty behaviours previously only reachable deliberately: a large container expands one line per element (print(buffer) costs a line per byte), and nesting recurses uncapped. print now passes PRINT_DATA_BOUNDS (maxLength 100, maxDepth 16). Bounds belong to the convenience path, which formats whatever it is handed; a caller who built a Pretty has seen their data and still gets no defaults. Both bounds announce themselves ('... +N', '{...}'), so truncation is visible. maxDepth is new on PrettyOptions, unbounded by default. Map and Set gained the '... +N' marker arrays and objects already had.

The cap did not work when first written, and that is the substantive change. _format's 'depth' carried two meanings: output indentation, and depth in the data. The compact probe passes depth 0 (correct for layout, since a single-line form has no indentation), so 'depth >= maxDepth' never fired down the probe path and a 400-deep object still hung. They are now separate fields on a Frame: 'inset' resets, 'level' only increases. [LAW:types-are-the-program]

Also replaces the console-highlighter test, which the reviewer correctly showed proved nothing: ReprHighlighter styles the number in { a: 1 } too, so it passed whether or not forwarding worked. It now records what the console's highlighter was handed.

KNOWN, NOT FIXED, NOT FILED: Pretty._formatObject formats every child twice (compact probe, then expanded), so cost is exponential in nesting depth. Measured on pre-existing code: depth 10=1ms, 20=17ms, 24=166ms, ~30=seconds. Pre-existing and still reachable via new Pretty(deep); print is now bounded by maxDepth 16 so the hazard is closed on the path this PR opened. Real fix: compute each child's single-line form once. Wants its own ticket and review.

* fix(pretty): let foreign data fail in place, and bound the third way it is large

Round-3 review findings, all on the same seam: `print` now hands arbitrary
data to `Pretty`, and `Pretty` reflects on values it did not create.

Reading foreign data can throw, and enumerating where showed the reviewer's
getter was one row of six. Compared against what `String(item)` did before
this PR: a property getter, `Object.keys`/Proxy `ownKeys`, a Proxy `get`, and
a Map/Set iterator were all unreachable and now throw; only `toString` and an
array index getter threw before. `String()` was simply the only reflection
the old code performed, which is why five of the six are new.

So the marker is one function and the catches are two, split by what a failed
read costs. A value that will not be read degrades alone, in `_property`, so
`{ a: 1, b: [Threw: not ready], c: 3 }` still shows what could be read. A
shape that will not be read leaves nothing to enumerate, so the container
degrades whole. The message travels into the output either way:
[LAW:no-silent-failure] is satisfied by the failure being visible and
attributed, not by it being fatal, and a marker naming its cause is not an
answer-shaped void. This supersedes the round-1 pushback that refused a
fallback for a throwing `toString` — that argument was right that the row was
not a regression and blind to the five rows beside it. Said so on the thread.

`PRINT_DATA_BOUNDS` gains `maxString: 1000`. A value is large in three ways
and the bound covered two: `print({ body: responseText })` embedded 50 KB
verbatim. Only strings nested in data are capped; a string argument is the
caller naming that string, and is printed in full.

`indexedElements` returns `ArrayLike` rather than a materialised array,
because an array and a typed array both already are one. Converting boxed
every element of a `Buffer` to keep the first hundred — bounding the output
while leaving the cost of producing it unbounded. A 20 MB `Uint8Array` now
prints in 4ms instead of allocating a 20-million-element array.

`Console.print` passes `indentGuides: doHighlight`. Guides are styling, so
`highlight: false` emitted ANSI the caller had declined, contradicting
docs/pretty.md. The console owns what `highlight` means for everything it
emits; the alternative was `Pretty` type-sniffing its own highlighter to
recover a decision the caller had already made.

CLAUDE.md's pretty bullet points at the module header instead of restating
three of its clauses verbatim, matching how the sanctioned-edge bullets point
at `why` in test/seam/layering.ts. [LAW:one-source-of-truth]

* fix(pretty): bound both containers and read both containers per position

Round-4 review findings. Three of the four are the same mistake: round 3
hardened one arm of a pair and left its sibling, so the arms disagreed about
things they should have agreed on.

Map and Set drained their iterators before `maxLength` applied — the eager
materialisation the array arm had just been reworked to avoid, two arms
below it. A 5,000-entry Map pulled 5,001 entries to show five. `take` stops
at the bound, and `.size` gives the total without iterating, so the `... +N`
remainder stays exact while the walk becomes O(maxLength).

The array arm read every kept index through one `slice`, so a single throwing
accessor propagated to the container's catch and cost the whole sequence:
`[1, <throws>, 3]` rendered `[Threw: boom]`. "array index getter" was row six
of the enumeration in the previous commit, and only the object arm was
hardened for it. `_property` becomes `_at`, taking a key or an index, because
reading one slot of a container someone else built is one job with two
spellings. [LAW:one-type-per-behavior] Arrays now read per position, and one
bad index costs `[1, [Threw: boom], 3]`.

The test pinning the typed-array fix was worse than absent, and the reviewer
caught it. It wrapped `Uint8Array` in a Proxy, but `ArrayBuffer.isView` is a
brand check on an internal slot and does not unwrap a Proxy the way
`Array.isArray` does, so the value never reached the arm under test. It fell
through to `String(value)`, `%TypedArray%.prototype.join` threw on an
incompatible receiver, and the `[Threw: …]` handling added in that same commit
turned the error into a pass. Every read count stayed 0 and the assertion held
for a reason unrelated to the bound. It now asserts what the fix is for — heap
growth while formatting a real 20MB `Uint8Array` — against the ~195MB the old
conversion cost. All three new tests were run against the reverted code first
and confirmed to fail.

docs/console.md now states the bounds `print` applies, that they are `print`'s
and not the formatter's, and that a string argument is never truncated. They
were surprising, silent, and written down nowhere a user reads.

* docs(pretty): say what happens when data refuses to be read

The `[Threw: …]` behaviour shipped in this PR was written down only in the
tests. A reader who hands `Pretty` an object with a lazy field met the marker
with no warning, and had no way to learn why one bad getter costs a single
entry while an unenumerable Proxy costs the whole container.

Sits beside the self-description and circular-reference paragraphs, which are
the same subject: what reflection does when it does not go as planned.

* fix(pretty): make the remainder marker an item, not a suffix

Found reviewing my own diff. The Map and Set arms push `... +N` onto the parts
list, and so does every expanded path; only the two compact paths glued it on
after a separator they assumed was already there. With `maxLength: 0` the
separator has nothing to follow, so an array rendered `[, ... +3]` and an
object `{ , ... +2 }` while a Map correctly rendered `Map {... +1}`.

Pre-existing, and it became an inconsistency when the Map arm was rewritten
one commit ago — the same arms-disagree shape as the last two rounds, which
is why it is worth the round rather than a follow-up ticket.

The marker is one more piece in the sequence now, so the separator is the
join's business in all four places. [LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow]

fix(markup): settle what a legal plugin tag name is, once (rich-markup-pwr) (#89)

A registered plugin name matched as a bare PREFIX of the tag text, and the
failure was silent in both directions.

Registering `table` destroyed every `table.*` built-in: `[table.header]x[/table.header]`
fired the plugin and dropped the `.header` as attributes. The mirror case:
`register("a.b")` succeeded but `[a.b]` could never reach the handler, because
the tag scan stops at the dot.

Both ends wanted the same answer to "what is a legal plugin tag name?" and
neither asked it. There is now one source fragment, anchored two ways:

- MATCH: `^(name)(?=$|[ \t])` — a registered name addresses a plugin only when
  the tag text ends there or continues with the whitespace that introduces
  attributes. `[table.header]` and `[table=x]` fall through to the built-in
  dialect exactly as an unregistered name would.
- REGISTER: `^name$` — a name markup could never address is rejected loudly
  instead of installing an unreachable handler.

The two anchorings are mirrors: every name `register` accepts is one the match
site can reach, and every name it rejects is unreachable.

The six-line hand scanner it replaces is gone; `register` keeps its existing
reserved-name guard, which asked a different question (is this itself a valid
style?) and could not have caught either case.

fix(cells): make chopCells advance on a glyph it cannot split (rich-cells-pfs) (#88)

* fix(cells): make chopCells advance on a glyph it cannot split

chopCells looped forever when a single glyph was wider than the whole
budget, then died with `RangeError: Invalid array length`. It drove the
loop with splitText, which pads to land exactly on the requested column
and hands the unsplittable glyph back untouched — so at a 1-cell budget
`chopCells("日本語", 1)` pushed a padded blank line and a remainder that
never shrank, forever. A terminal reporting a 1-cell width is enough to
reach it, and cc-candybar already floors its fold budget at 2 cells to
route around it.

Drive the loop with cellFitFrom over code-unit offsets instead, taking
`max(fit, nextCodePoint)`: nextCodePoint is always strictly past the
start, so the loop advances by construction rather than by a guard, and
the case where nothing fits force-takes the glyph and lets it overflow
by its own width — the only answer that both terminates and keeps the
text intact. cellFit already documents that its caller must choose
between force-taking and skipping; chopCells now chooses.

Side effect worth naming: chopCells no longer pads. It is a chopping
function, `join("") === input` now holds for every input, and a line
that stops short of a wide glyph is narrower than maxWidth rather than
padded out to it. splitText keeps its padding — that is its job.

* refactor(cells): give the force-take rule one home in cellStepFrom

The "fit what you can, and take one glyph anyway when nothing fits" rule
lived in two places with two spellings: charGreedyWrap in the textarea,
and the loop chopCells just grew. That is not a hypothetical drift risk
— the copies had already drifted, and the drift is the bug the previous
commit fixed: the textarea force-took, chopCells did neither and hung.

Extract cellStepFrom beside cellFitFrom and route both callers through
it. Not exported from the barrel: it is an internal seam between core/
and widgets/, and a new public export is carrying cost plus a
coverage-gate obligation with no consumer asking for it.

charGreedyWrap sheds a dead guard on the way — `if (end === pos) break;`
after nextCodePoint was unreachable, since the loop condition already
guarantees pos < line.length. Its `cap <= 0` guard stays put: a
zero-width row budget is the textarea's concern, not the step
primitive's.

Also scope chopCells' overflow bound to what it can actually promise.
The docstring claimed the only line exceeding maxWidth is one overwide
glyph, which the `maxWidth <= 0` return breaks by handing back the whole
string. Both cases are one rule — a line overflows exactly where the
budget cannot be met — and saying it that way is shorter than the
version that was wrong.

* docs(cells): scope cellStepFrom's advance guarantee to inside the text

The docstring claimed cellStepFrom never returns startCU. At
text.length it does, and correctly so — nothing is left to take, and
that total behavior is what lets both callers drive their loop with no
special case at the end.

The first draft said "for any startCU inside text," which was true; the
pass that shortened it to "never returns startCU" is what dropped the
precondition. Restoring the qualifier and naming the loop shape the
termination argument actually covers.

test(docs): follow the receivers a static factory produces (rich-docs-site-13t.6.5) (#87)

A variable was recorded only when its initializer was `new X()`, so a name
bound from a static factory entered no declaration list, resolved to no root,
and every member called on it was dropped without a report. `docs/tables.md`'s
whole grid section and `docs/style.md`'s `Style.parse` section were outside the
gate, and a ghost method on either would have passed.

A binding now carries the receiver chain its initializer describes rather than
a class name, which is the same thing `describeReceiver` already computed for
a use — the guard was discarding an answer the parser had in hand. Resolution
follows those chains back recursively, and a bare imported name the page
declared nothing for resolves to the class object itself. A class has two
member sets, instance and statics, and only step zero of a chain may read the
static one; everything after a factory is an instance again.

Widening the gate found two things the old one could not see. `RichText.fromAnsi`
does not exist and never has, so `docs/text.md`'s "Building from ANSI codes"
section is deleted rather than implemented. `docs/console.md` binds `output` to
an array in one section and to `console.endCapture()` in another, which surfaced
a hole the widening opened: a declaration that binds nothing followable still
takes the name, or the fallback-forward rule hands it an unrelated declaration
elsewhere on the page.

Both static-factory forms are pinned by fixtures rather than by the corpus.
Reverting the guard alone leaves all 37 corpus tests green and turns four
fixtures red, which is the whole argument for having them.

Also: `docs/live.md` claimed a file-based console emits only when "the context"
exits. There is no context on that page any more, and the claim was false in
both halves — `Live` never checks whether its console is a terminal and writes
every frame it draws. And `docs/.vitepress/sidebar.ts` claimed the reachability
check has no exclusion predicate; `test/docs/pages.ts` has one on the disk
side, so the claim is now scoped to the sidebar side it is true of.

* test(docs): gate the two lies a machine can catch, and name the one it cannot

Adds the last child of the docs-site epic: a check that every symbol the
documentation names exists, and every page the site ships is reachable.

REACHABILITY is a set equality with no exclusions. `docs/strip.md` was
unreachable for four commits because the sidebar was a hand-copied list and
nobody could see the drift by reading either file. The page-backed regions move
to `docs/.vitepress/sidebar.ts` so the test can import the site's own list

a member called on a class the page itself constructed. The second is what
catches the transliteration defects, since six of this epic's confirmed ghosts
were methods rather than imports. Both derive from `package.json#exports`
through the coverage gate's own `deriveEntryModules`, now returning specifier →
source rather than discarding the specifier, so "exists" means the same thing in
both directions.

that way would have failed every page using it, and the obvious fix would have
looked like "stop re-exporting". `origins` is keyed by declaration identity.

* docs(console): describe the eight methods Console has, not the fourteen it doesn't (rich-docs-site-13t.4)

The ticket named `logLocals`. The page carried twenty-two false claims.

`Console`'s real surface is eight methods: print, log, rule, printJson,
beginCapture, endCapture, exportText, exportHtml. The page documented six
members that do not exist — `out`, `status`, `input`, `screen`, `pager`, and a
static `Console.capture()` — across five sections and two blocks that declared
`const console` twice, which would be a SyntaxError if run.

Three of those six are real capabilities documented on the wrong object. This
port moved several of Python Rich's Console methods to standalone classes, and
the docs were never told, so `status`, `input` and `screen` redirect to
`Status`, `Prompt` and `Live` rather than being deleted. `out` and `pager` have
no implementation anywhere and are gone.

The rest could not have been caught by any type checker, because every one of
them type-checks clean:

- `logLocals` is not configuration. `print()` sniffs its last argument for known
  option keys, so an unrecognized options object is demoted to a value to print,
  stringified to `[object Object]`, and eaten by the markup parser. It prints
  nothing — not, as the ticket assumed, a literal object.
- Printing or logging a plain object hits that same swallow and yields a blank
  line. The page claimed both were pretty-printed.
- `log()` adds a timestamp and nothing else; there is no location column.
- `rule()` does not parse markup in its title.
- `printJson` re-indents but does not colorize, while `print()` of the same
  string does.
- `crop`, `justify: "left"`, `justify: "full"` and `overflow: "ignore"` are
  accepted and inert.
- `NO_COLOR` strips bold along with colour, contradicting the page.
- The colour-system table listed two specs that throw, omitted the two that
  work, and gave the Windows palette as 8 colours where it has 16.

Every claim above was verified by executing it against a width-pinned console
and capturing stdout, and every code block on the page now type-checks against
`src/`.

Filed rather than fixed here: rich-console-nac (four inert PrintOptions),
rich-console-8lg (printJson's sortKeys silently no-ops via a cast to the
replacer parameter, and its missing highlighting), rich-docs-site-dl4
(docs/live.md documents `screen:`/`live.run()`/`new Table("a","b")`, none of
