* docs(console): an object's keys decide whether print takes it as data or options

Two corrections from review, both verified by execution.

The colour-spec claim was generalized from two samples. `STRING_TO_DEPTH` in
`src/core/color.ts` is one table serving configuration and detection both, so
`resolveColorSystem` accepts every FORCE_COLOR value and every terminal
identifier detection knows: `{ colorSystem: "vscode" }` silently means
truecolor, `"true"` means ansi, `"0"` means none. Only strings outside the whole
table throw. The page said any string but the five throws.

`log()`'s trailing argument is not simply a value. It forwards to `print()`,
which sniffs the last argument for the nine `PrintOptions` names, so whether an
object is data or configuration depends on its keys. `end` is one of the nine
and it sets the line terminator, which makes the worst case visible rather than
silent: `console.log("range", { end: "2024" })` emits `range2024` with no
newline. The page asserted a trailing object is always printed as a value.

Both are cases where the type checker sees nothing wrong, which is why neither
turned up in the per-block tsc pass.

renderToString is exported from the main barrel and renders any Renderable to

* docs(pretty): pin the width the examples were captured at, and stop overclaiming maxLength

Review caught that the page named a console width of 43 while every snippet
constructed a bare `new Console()`. The default is 80 (console.ts:196, `w || 80`),

showed the expanded one. Every snippet now passes `{ width: 43 }`.

The cause is worth naming because it is the same one review caught twice on #82:
I verified in a configuration that did not share the assumption under test. My
harness rewrote `new Console()` into `new Console({ width: 43, record: true })` so
it could capture output — and that rewrite is exactly what made the outputs true
in the harness and false on the page, the way `as never` did for the generator
claim last time. The blocks are now re-extracted with the `@promptctl/rich-js`
specifier as the only edit, and stdout is captured by swapping
`process.stdout.write` rather than by constructing a different Console.

`maxLength` was also described as if it annotated every container. It does not:
the array and plain-object branches compute `remaining` and append `... +N`, and
the `Map` and `Set` branches slice and stop. `new Pretty(map, { maxLength: 2 })`

fix(width): an unbounded width means render at your natural width (rich-width-3cf.5) (#79)

* fix(width): an unbounded width means render at your natural width (rich-width-3cf.5)

`Panel`, `Padding`, `Columns` and `Layout` threw at `maxWidth: Infinity` —
each expands into the width it is offered, so each reached
`" ".repeat(Infinity)`, and `Columns` reached `new Array(Infinity)` as well
because its column count comes off the width too. The ticket asked what a
renderable should emit into an unbounded canvas, and left it open on purpose:
the answer had to be one answer, not four.

It is: an unbounded offer means "render at your natural width", and the
natural width is what `measure` already reports. `withBoundedWidth` in
`protocol.ts` is the single checkpoint — it parses like `withCellWidth`, then
resolves an unbounded offer by asking the renderable it was handed. It sits at
the top of `render` and never at the top of `measure`, which would ask the
question with itself.

THREE RENDERABLES HAD NO NATURAL WIDTH TO REPORT. `Tree`, `Columns` and
`Layout` all answered `measure` with `maximum = the offer`. That is why
"consult measure rather than filling" could not work as written, and it was
never only an `Infinity` problem: `Panel {expand: false}` around a Tree at
width 40 drew a 40-cell frame around nine cells of tree. Each now reports what
its content wants — Tree the widest row its own walk emits, Columns one row of
every item, Layout its children laid out the way its split lays them out — and
`test/renderables/natural-width.test.ts` holds that end at ordinary widths.

Two more found on the way. `Panel.measure` ignored a declared `width`, so it
reported nine cells while `render` drew twelve; both now read one accessor.
`Table.measure` let `UNBOUNDED` (its own `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` infinity) escape as
a number — a column declared `{ratio: Infinity}` measured 18014398509481988 and
rendered `RangeError: Invalid string length` out of the top border.

Content that cannot measure itself has no natural width, and `withBoundedWidth`
throws a `RangeError` naming the cause rather than losing the content silently
or guessing a number. The width sweep pins which configurations those are, so a
renderable that quietly stops reporting a natural width fails the suite instead
of joining the list.

Verified: reverting any one of the six changed renderables fails between one
and six of the new assertions; none are inert. `npm test` 2018 green,
`npm run lint` clean, `npm run docs:build` clean, `npm run test:demos` 10/10.

`withBoundedWidth` is exported from the barrel and documented in
docs/protocol.md's width contract, which — with `cellCount`'s header and the
sweep's header — is the third of the three texts that named this ticket.


* fix(width): derive the natural width from the allocator, not beside it

Review found the same law broken in four places, and it is the law this
PR was most exposed to: `_naturalWidth` is a second map of a fact the
allocator already owns, so the two diverged, and they diverged exactly
where the PR aimed — rendering at your own reported natural width
cropped your own content.

`Layout` row splits summed what each child wants. `_distributeSpace`
does not hand out a sum; it hands each flex child `floor(budget * ratio
/ totalRatio)` off one shared budget. So `splitRow("left", "right")`
reported 9 and then rendered `"leftrigh" / "    t"` at 9, because
`floor(9/2)` is 4 and "right" is five cells. The inverse of that rule is
`want * totalRatio / ratio` and the row needs the *largest* demand, not
the total: a 1:1 split cannot give one pane five cells without giving
the other five too, so the honest answer is 10.

`Layout` also answered "am I a leaf" twice — `render` off `_children`,
`_naturalWidth` off the *visible* children. A layout holding content and
one hidden child reported twelve cells and rendered nothing, and a
fit-mode `Panel` framed twelve cells of air. Leafness now has one home
that both read.

`Columns` auto mode sized columns at a flat four cells while reporting a
natural width built from the items, so six two-cell items claimed 22 and
wrapped into two rows at 22. Auto now derives its column count from
`_itemWidth` the way `equal` already does, which makes the existing
shared formula its exact inverse — at `count*itemWidth + gutter*(count-1)`
the expression collapses to `count`, one row, by identity. That removes
the divergence rather than adding a third formula for it, and `_divide`'s
`[LAW:single-enforcer]` header claim is now true where auto quietly
disagreed.

`docs/protocol.md`'s reference `measure()` returned `Measurement(1, 0)`
for a widget with no lines — a floor above its own ceiling, the exact
defect the prose two paragraphs below forbids. The floor now comes off
the clamped ceiling, which is what every renderable in `src/` already
does.

All four passed the suite before this commit. `natural-width.test.ts`
asserted cell counts only, and a cell count is what a renderable that
crops itself still gets right — `Panel`'s padding absorbed the
shortfall, so the totals agreed while the pane inside them wrapped. It
now also reads the text, per case, as the rows that must survive
together; two cases were added for the shapes that never showed the bug
(items narrower than a column, panes at unequal ratios).

Verified: reverting columns.ts fails 1 assertion, reverting layout.ts
fails 3, none inert. `npm test` 2031 green, `npm run lint` clean,
`npm run docs:build` clean, `npm run test:demos` 10/10.


* fix(width): a pane that does not grow is paid, not divided by

Review round two. The headline is a regression I shipped in 5411a676:
`_rowBudgetFor` inverted the ratio rule by dividing by `child.ratio`,
and `LayoutOptions.ratio` is an unvalidated `number` that admits 0. I
derived the inverse from the algebra of the forward rule instead of
from its domain. `splitRow(Layout("x", {ratio: 0}))` measured
`{NaN, NaN}`; with a growing sibling it measured `Infinity`, which
`measure` clamped into "I want the whole offer" — the exact lie the
method exists to remove.

Fixing only the inverse could not work. With a zero-ratio child inside
the ratio pass there is no budget the forward rule honours: panes of
`zzz`/`aaaaa`/`bbbbb` consume `3 + 2*floor(T/2)` cells out of `T`, which
no `T` satisfies, because the child draws its `minimumSize` from a
budget the shares have already spent. It came out right at 16 only
because the trailing `Math.min(remaining, ...)` clipped the last share
to the right number.

So `_distributeSpace` changes: a `ratio` of 0 is the caller saying this
pane does not grow, so it is paid its `minimumSize` alongside the
fixed-`size` panes and the ratio budget is what remains, divided among
the panes that do. Every ratio reaching the division is now positive, so
the degenerate case stops being representable rather than being
guarded, and `_rowBudgetFor` inverts that directly. The example above
now needs 13 cells rather than 16.

Three more, all one law.

`Table.render` had `this._geometry(this.tableWidth ?? options.maxWidth)`
while `measure` bounded the same two fields by the offer — two
expressions for one fact, and the wrong one on the path that draws
bytes. `new Table({width: Infinity})` with a `{ratio: 1}` column threw
`RangeError: Invalid string length` at an ordinary 80-cell offer,
walking straight past the width `withBoundedWidth` had just resolved.
Both now read `_outerWidth`, which also parses the declared width as a
cell count instead of storing it raw.

THAT DECIDES `rich-table-width-y1a`, WHICH ASKED WHETHER A DECLARED
TABLE WIDTH SHOULD CLAMP TO ITS CONTAINER. It does now. `Panel` already
clamped its own declared width, upstream Rich bounds a table by the
console, and the alternative is a 40-cell table soft-wrapping in a
12-cell console and destroying the frame of everything printed after.
The sweep was written for this outcome — it gains both declared-width
configurations and loses the header note that excluded them. `Columns`
has the same defect, has no finding against it here, and stays on the
ticket.

`Panel.measure` treated a declared width as a ceiling on a
content-derived range while `_getPanelWidth` returns it outright before
measuring anything: `{width: 20}` around "hi" offered 100 cells answered
6..20 and drew 20 every time, so a parent dividing from the floor
under-provisioned it. A declared width now answers both ends, stated
once above the split rather than patched into both arms — which lets
`declared ?? ...` fall out of both.

`layoutPanel`'s `cellCount(outerWidth)` and the comment justifying it
are gone. All three call sites hand it an integer now that
`_declaredWidth` parses upstream, and a wrong comment is fixed by
shrinking it. `docs/protocol.md`'s "Every built-in renderable begins
this way" is attributed per method, since `render` begins with
`withBoundedWidth` in all six.

Verified: reverting layout.ts fails 7 of the new assertions, panel.ts 1,
table.ts 2. `npm test` 2053 green, `npm run lint` clean, `npm run
docs:build` clean, `npm run test:demos` 10/10. One pre-existing caveat:
`test/seam/browser-safe.test.ts` times out at its 5s limit under this
machine's load average of 75 — it passes in isolation in 4.1s and times
out identically on an unmodified tree, so it is load, not this change.


* fix(width): a declared size is a cell count, parsed where it arrives

Layout.size/minimumSize are cell counts supplied as plain numbers that
never meet withCellWidth. Harmless while Layout.measure was always an
integer; _rowBudgetFor made them load-bearing, so size:5.5 measured 6.5
and size:-5 measured -4. Parsed in the constructor now, absence
preserved, matching Columns' colWidth checkpoint.

The sink is a regression I introduced in 8cf549c6 by deleting
layoutPanel's cellCount(outerWidth) as dead. It was not: _getPanelWidth
derives the fit width from Measurement.get on an arbitrary Measurable,
so a negative maximum reached String.repeat and threw RangeError:
Invalid count value: -15. Restored with the live reason. cellCount
returns a branded CellCol, which makes that a border checkpoint, not an
inland guard [LAW:parse-dont-validate]; the stale comment named the
wrong border, it did not remove the border.

Left for its own ticket: Measurement.get is the documented single
enforcer yet lets negative/fractional measurements through, with
normalize() unused on that path.

Verified: reverting layout.ts fails 6 new assertions, panel.ts 1.
npm test 2060 green, lint clean, docs:build clean, test:demos 10/10.
browser-safe.test.ts times out at 5s under this machine's load,
identically on an unmodified tree; passes in isolation in 4.1s.


* fix(width): a measurement that crossed the enforcer is stamped

`Measurement.get` carried a comment naming it the single entry point for
measuring a `Measurable`, capped the maximum against the offer, and enforced
nothing else — while `Measurement.normalize`, which floors a negative range and
un-inverts a minimum above its own maximum, sat two methods above it with no
caller anywhere in src/.

So each consumer met an arbitrary `Measurable`'s bad numbers itself. `Panel`
returned a public `{-16, -16}` for content reporting `{-20, -20}`; a `Layout`
leaf returned `{-20, -20}`. `Columns`, `Tree` and the `Layout` row path escaped
only because each happens to seed its `Math.max` from a non-negative number —
one missing guarantee wearing four coincidences.

Stamping it at the checkpoint makes it a guarantee, and is why no consumer
carries a floor of its own. Fractions are untouched: `normalize` clamps and
un-inverts, and what a fractional maximum should mean stays an open question.


* fix(width): the one measure() that walked around the checkpoint

`Table.measure` took `rawOptions.maxWidth` straight into `_outerWidth` and
`layoutTable`, the only `measure` in the library not beginning at
`withCellWidth` — while `Table.render`, ten lines up, parses through
`withBoundedWidth` before calling the same `_outerWidth`. One helper, two input
contracts, decided by which caller you arrived from.

It reported sane numbers regardless, because `layoutTable` floors the width
again internally. That is the reason to fix it rather than to leave it: the
protection belongs to a different function's contract, sits one call deep, and
docs/protocol.md tells readers that every built-in `measure` begins at the
checkpoint. A pattern that holds five times out of six cannot be relied on, and
the sixth is the one nobody checks.

Behaviour is unchanged today, which is why the tests assert the contract rather
than which call enforces it — they survive either point moving and fail if both
go.


* fix(width): a ratio is a share weight, parsed where it arrives

`size` and `minimumSize` were parsed at the constructor last round; `ratio` is
the third `LayoutOptions` number doing width arithmetic and was still taken raw.
It became load-bearing in what `measure` reports when a row learned to answer
with the budget its panes need, so an unparsed one stopped being a layout
mistake and escaped as a measurement.

Two ways out. `ratio: NaN` made `totalRatio` NaN and the whole measurement NaN.
A negative ratio summed with its siblings to a `totalRatio` of 0, so a row
holding twelve cells of text reported a natural width of 0 — while
`_distributeSpace`, dividing by the same ratios at render time, handed both
panes real space. Measure and render disagreeing is the pair this epic exists to
make inverses of each other.

Not `cellCount`: a ratio of 2.5 divides space perfectly well and flooring it
would be wrong. A weight that cannot name a share — negative, NaN, infinite —
reads as 0 instead, which already means "this pane does not grow" and is
filtered out before any division. That is what makes the claim above
`_distributeSpace` that every ratio reaching it is positive true by
construction; it was simply false before, and named as such in review.


* fix(width): a container crops what its content will not

The sweep gained a `Layout` wrapping content that ignores its width, and a
`Tree` whose label does — the two places this epic grew the unmeasurable-content
fallback without pinning it. Both configurations failed the sweep's oldest
assertion immediately, at every width, not only the unbounded one they were
added for: forty cells emitted into a one-cell offer.

Neither cropped. A `Layout` leaf forwarded the offer to its content and yielded
whatever came back; `Tree` fitted its guides with `cellFit` and then trusted the
label. `Panel`, `Padding` and `Table` split and adjust, which is why the same
content stays inside its offer there and why the defect never surfaced — no
configuration had ever handed the other two a renderable that lies.

`Segment.cropLines` is that step, next to `adjustLineLength`, which already
holds the rule for a single line. A container holding arbitrary content has a
stream of lines and no way to make one call do it, which is how both of these
came to trust content instead. For a layout it is not cosmetic: a pane wider
than its region overwrites the pane beside it.


* docs(protocol): a max over a collection accumulates, never spreads

The canonical `measure()` example computed its natural width with
`Math.max(0, ...this.lines.map(cellLen))`, passing one argument per line. A
widget backed by a large enough array — a log viewer, a file preview, exactly
what the example models — overruns the engine's argument limit and throws
`RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` out of `measure()`, on ordinary
oversized input rather than any malformed width.

`Tree` and `Columns` both loop for this reason, so the reference implementation
was teaching the one pattern the library itself declined to use — and the doc is
the half a reader copies.


* fix(width): parse at the border in the places round 5 found

* test(width): the new ratio config has no natural width either

"Table at a declared unbounded width with a ratio column" was added in
06fe4525 to give the crash-path comment above it a config that can
actually reach the crash. Like "Table with an unbounded column demand"
it asks for an unbounded width itself, so it has no natural width to
fall back on and the unbounded-offer assertion cannot hold for it.

Being in the set only exempts that one assertion; the finite widths
still sweep it, which is where the clamp this epic added matters.


* test(width): pin the five fixes round 5 made at the border

Each fix in 06fe4525 moved a parse to the boundary that owns it, and each
was reachable from a public API. These reach them the same way a caller
would, so the fix cannot be reverted quietly:

- `cropLines` shortens and does not count — asserted from both sides, a
  stream gaining no terminator it did not emit and an empty line keeping
  the one it did, plus the zero-width line that is present rather than
  absent. Both wrong shapes of it failed exactly one of those.
- A `Tree` label with nothing in it still gets a row, so the next row's
  guides do not land on it.
- `normalize` reads NaN as no cells and leaves an unbounded maximum
  unbounded — the asymmetry is the point, since flooring both is what
  would trade `withBoundedWidth`'s RangeError for a silent zero.
- A declared `Padding` side is a quantity, so the unbounded width an
  offer may carry means nothing there.
- The three declared `Layout` numbers parse on assignment, which is the
  only way the guarantee survives a caller reaching a pane by name.

Reverting each source file in turn fails these and nothing else: measure
2, segment 7, tree 1, padding 1, layout 2.

test(width): sweep every renderable across the widths nobody tests (rich-width-3cf.3) (#78)

* test(width): sweep every renderable across the widths nobody tests (rich-width-3cf.3)

The standing guard for the epic: one sweep, applied to a table of fifteen
configurations across Panel, Table, Tree, Columns and Layout, asserting that
none of them emits a line wider than the width it was given at any width from
0 to 20 — and that a fractional or non-numeric width renders exactly as its
floor.

The sweep found that three of the five renderables did not hold, so this
commit also makes them hold.

WHAT THE ASSERTIONS ARE FOR. Each is here because a bound alone was measured
to miss a real bug. A renderable that emits nothing satisfies "no line exceeds
the width" — `RichText` with the default `ellipsis` overflow emitted zero
lines at maxWidth 1, which is why a hard-squeezed table looked blank rather
than truncated. A broken frame's content rows are narrower than its border,
not wider — padding 1.5 on a Panel gave [13, 11, 13]. And a width that is not
an integer corrupts output without exceeding anything. So: at least one line,
rows that agree for renderables that draw a frame, a measured range a parent
can divide, and equality against a reference render.

THE ONE SENTENCE THE CODE NEVER SAID. Every failure was the same fact stated
nowhere: maxWidth is a count of cells, so a non-negative integer. `table.ts`
said it in `cells()`, `padding.ts` said it again in `side()`, `panel.ts`
approximated it with `Math.max(1, ...)`, and `text.ts`, `tree.ts`,
`columns.ts` and `layout.ts` never said it at all — so they disagreed. At NaN,
Table collapsed to one cell of garbage, Columns and Layout threw `Invalid
array length`, and RichText ignored the request and emitted its full natural
width.

Now `cellCount` in `core/cells.ts` is the only place that rule lives, and
`withCellWidth` in `core/protocol.ts` is the checkpoint every renderable
crosses. It returns options rather than a number on purpose: parsing into a
local leaves the caller's raw value in `options` for whatever the renderable
forwards it to. Columns was fixed that way first and still threw, because it
handed the unparsed original to `Measurement.get`.

The two RichText questions the ticket asked to be decided once:

- fold into a zero-cell canvas emits the bare line terminator, the same as
  crop and ellipsis, instead of stepping by zero forever (~2^27 pushes and a
  gigabyte before a RangeError).
- ellipsis at maxWidth 1 emits the marker. The `maxWidth > 1` guard that stood
  there was a guard with no else over arithmetic that was already correct at
  1; deleting it is the whole fix.

Tree had the epic's defect verbatim: it emitted its guides and then handed the
label `options` unchanged, so the label was told it had the whole outer width
while the guides had already spent four cells of it. Both call sites now route
through one `_renderRow` that divides the width once. Layout applied each
child's `minimumSize` independently of the budget, so two children asked to
fit one cell merged into a two-cell row.

`maxWidth: Infinity` is deliberately outside the sweep and still throws in
Panel, Columns and Layout. The epic's invariant is trivially true there, and
the crash is an expansion defect rather than a squeeze; deciding what every
renderable renders at an unbounded width is worth doing on purpose, so it is
filed rather than smuggled in behind a clamp.


* docs(protocol): state what a width means, once (rich-width-3cf.3)

`docs/protocol.md` described `RenderOptions.maxWidth` only as "width and other
context", so an author of a custom renderable had nowhere to learn what the
number means at the bottom of its range — which is the regime the whole
`rich-width-3cf` epic lives in.

It now says: a count of cells, every emitted line fits inside it, a negative
width and NaN both mean zero, a fractional width is floored, zero is a real
request, and `measure` carries the same ceiling.

The `MyWidget` example is fixed in the same pass because it taught the defect:
`return new Measurement(10, 40)` ignores `options.maxWidth` entirely and
reports a minimum above its own maximum as soon as the offer drops below 10.
That is exactly the bug `Columns` and `Layout` had, and a reader copying the
example inherited it.


* fix(padding): divide the requested width once, so no row can overflow it

`Padding` had the defect the rest of this epic fixed, and the sweep this
branch adds did not cover it — so it shipped a guard with a hole where
one of the renderables it guards used to be.

It derived its geometry three times and clamped each derivation
differently. `render` took the canvas as `Math.max(1, maxWidth - left -
right)`, which clamps *up*: a padding of 1 inside a 2-cell request drew
3-cell content rows beside 2-cell blank rows, an open frame the terminal
then soft-wraps. `blankLine` came off the raw `maxWidth`, so a negative
width reached `" ".repeat` and threw `RangeError: Invalid count value:
-5` — publicly reachable as `renderToString(new Padding(x, 1), { width:
-5 })`. `measure` derived it a third time and reported a range past the
offer in both directions:

    Padding.measure({maxWidth: -5})           {minimum: 2, maximum: -5}
    new Padding(x, 3).measure({maxWidth: 2})  {minimum: 8, maximum: 8}

`layoutPadding` now divides the requested width once into left, content
and right, summing to exactly it, with `cellCount` at that single
division point. Content takes its first cell before padding takes any,
matching `layoutPanel`: a squeeze should cost the decoration, not the
thing being decorated. `render` and `measure` both read that division,
so they cannot disagree again.

Content rows route through `Segment.adjustLineLength`, whose `pad` flag
is exactly what `expand` means — while its crop half runs unconditionally,
so a child that ignored the canvas it was handed cannot burst the padding
around it. That replaces the hand-rolled `remaining` arithmetic, and the
zero-length spans it leaves behind need no branch to suppress, since the
wire boundary drops empty segments.

Three `Padding` configurations join the sweep. Eleven of their twelve
assertions fail against the previous commit; the twelfth is the ragged
shape's deliberate no-op.

* fix(columns): parse a declared column width as the cell count it is

`Columns.render` parses `options.maxWidth` through `withCellWidth`, but
`this.colWidth` arrives by a different door — the constructor — and was
used raw. `new Columns(items, { width: NaN })` made `Math.max(1, NaN)` a
NaN column count and `new Array(NaN)` threw `RangeError: Invalid array
length` before a single column was laid out. `width: 4.5` laid out
fractional columns.

Same rule, same parser, applied where that door is: `cellCount` in the
constructor, as `Table` does for `col.width` via `demandCells`. Absence
is preserved rather than parsed — `undefined` selects auto-fit, and
`cellCount(undefined)` would read it as a declared zero and silently
reroute an auto Columns into the declared-width branch.

The tests live in columns.test.ts rather than the width sweep because a
Columns with a declared `width` legitimately overruns a narrower
`options.maxWidth`, the way a declared-width Table does
(`rich-table-width-y1a`), so the sweep's upper bound is the wrong
assertion for it. What does hold is the equivalence the sweep pins
elsewhere, asserted against a reference render: a declared NaN, -5 and
4.5 lay out as 0, 0 and 4. All three fail against the previous commit.

* docs(protocol): hand implementors the parser the width contract requires

The page asserted a contract and withheld the only tool that satisfies
it. `withCellWidth` was not exported, so its `MyWidget` example clamped
with `Math.min(10, options.maxWidth)` — which is `NaN` for a NaN width,
the exact bug the epic fixed internally, demonstrated as the pattern to
copy two paragraphs above the rule forbidding it.

`withCellWidth` joins the barrel and the example calls it. The
alternative — printing an inline `Number.isFinite(...) ? ... : 0` in the
prose — was refused: it mints a second copy of the parse rule where
nothing checks it against `cellCount`, which is this finding's own
failure mode one layer down. It already disagreed, mapping `Infinity` to
zero. `cellCount` itself stays internal; `withCellWidth(options).maxWidth`
is the ceiling a `measure` needs, and two doors onto one rule is how the
rule starts having two answers.

Exporting it is not merely convenient. The width checkpoint sits at each
render/measure entry because `render()` is public and every entry is a
real crossing — and a third-party `Renderable` is one of those entries.
The page also now says that nothing calls it on the implementor's
behalf, since `renderToString` forwards `options?.width` untouched.

`Infinity` was claimed as "not a supported width" beside a `cellCount`
comment calling an unbounded width "a legitimate request", which passes
it through unchanged. Two maps, one fact, opposite readings — and
neither was the territory: nothing in `src/` passes `Infinity` as a
maxWidth, `Table` modelling its own unboundedness as a deliberately
finite `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. Both texts now say what happens — it passes
the checkpoint unclamped, and the renderables that throw on it are the
open `rich-width-3cf.5` gap, not something the contract prevents. No
clamp was added, because there is no cell count that means unbounded and
picking one here would answer that ticket behind a checkpoint change.

Per test/coverage, the new value export needs a demo rather than an
allowlist entry, and `examples/shared/window.ts` is a custom renderable
that was breaking this very contract: its `measure` returned
`MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` regardless of the offer, a ceiling no parent could
divide against. It now parses and reports the offer, so the page's
worked example and the shipped one agree. Verified the gate by removing
the demo and watching it name the export.

* docs(protocol): make the width-contract example compile as written

The previous commit gave the `MyWidget` example a single import line for
`withCellWidth`. That was worse than the no-import fragment it replaced:
one import makes a block look self-contained, so a reader copies it and
finds `Renderable`, `Measurable`, `RenderOptions`, `Measurement` and
`Segment` all undefined.

Restored to the two-line form every other example on the page uses —
`import type` for the type-only names, `import` for the values — with
`Segment` and `Measurement` on the value line because both are classes,
matching the `Checkerboard` example directly above.

Checked rather than eyeballed: the block extracted verbatim, with the
package specifier repointed at the barrel, type-checks clean under
`--strict`.

* fix(panel): drop the content floor whose reason this branch removed

`_renderContent` rendered its child at `Math.max(1, contentWidth)`, and
the comment above it explained why: `RichText`'s fold walked a cursor
forward by `maxWidth`, so a zero-cell canvas spun ~2^27 pushes and about
a gigabyte before a `RangeError`.

That stopped being true earlier on this branch, when `text.ts` gained a
`maxWidth === 0` branch making the fold agree with `crop` and `ellipsis`
at the bottom of the range. The floor outlived its reason, and the
comment became the worst kind of stale: it told the next maintainer that
deleting the floor would reintroduce an infinite loop that was already
fixed three commits earlier. Removing the workaround is what the epic's
notes on this ticket predicted — "that floor is deletable, and deleting
it is arguably this ticket's job" — so the paragraph goes with it rather
than being rewritten into a defence of code that no longer needs one.

`contentWidth === 0 ? [] : lines` stays. It looks like part of the same
workaround and is not: it says a zero-cell canvas holds no rows, which
is still true and is what the surviving first paragraph already states.

That pairing is also why this is output-preserving by construction — at
zero the lines are discarded regardless, so the width handed to the
child only ever affected the child's internal work and the accessory
thunk the first paragraph describes. Verified rather than reasoned
about: 375 panel renders (5 child kinds x 5 option sets x 15 widths from
0 to 40, `RichText`/`Table`/`Tree` children included) are byte-identical
across the change.

fix(table): divide the requested width once, so no row can overflow it (rich-width-3cf.2) (#77)

* fix(table): divide the requested width once, so no row can overflow it (rich-width-3cf.2)

`Table` emitted rows at a width it picked without reference to the width it was
given. At every requested width from 1 to 13 the sample three-column table
rendered the same 13 cells, because the width was divided in three independent
places that could not agree: `_calculateWidths` subtracted borders and padding,
`_totalTableWidth` added them back, and five box-row callsites re-derived
`w + padLeft + padRight`. The `Math.max(1, ...)` floor in the first pinned every
column at one cell while the other two kept billing for padding that was no
longer affordable. The terminal soft-wraps such a row, and the wrap destroys the
frame of every renderable printed after it.

One `layoutTable(outerWidth, demands, padding, frame)` now returns fields that
sum to exactly the width it produced, and that width is never more than the one
requested. Every row reads from it: both borders, the header separator, the
section and footer rules, the data rows, and the title/caption spans.

Cells go out in the same priority order `Panel` uses — the pair of edge columns,
then one content cell per column with the divider in front of it, then the
padding, then the remainder back to content. A column the width cannot seat is
dropped rather than drawn outside the frame.

The remainder is apportioned a cell at a time by the highest-averages rule
rather than by proportional flooring, so the granted widths are exact with no
rounding residue for a second pass to sweep up, and per-column caps fall out for
free: a capped column stops winning rounds and its cells flow to the columns
that can use them. A declared `width` is a reservation paid before the bidding
rather than a weight competing in it — without that distinction a wide neighbour
wins every cell and a `width: 4` column renders one cell wide.

Also fixed, both found by following the geometry through:

- `measure({ maxWidth: 1 })` returned `{minimum: 6, maximum: 1}` — a floor above
  its own ceiling. Both ends are now widths the geometry produced, so the range
  cannot invert.
- `_renderTitle` cropped by code units, so a title of wide characters was up to
  twice the table's width on screen. It crops by cells now.

`Box.getTop`/`getRow`/`getBottom` take `readonly number[]`; they never mutated
the array, and dropping the constraint beats copying at four callsites.

Not changed here: `expand` is still accepted and unimplemented — wiring it up
needs `Progress` to put a ratio on its bar column first, or every progress row
gets three equal columns. Filed separately.


* fix(table): bound the width apportionment by column count, not by the width

`distribute` handed out cells one at a time, so its iteration count was the
requested width. A `ratio` column never reaches a cap, which left the loop
draining the budget alone — and `Infinity - 1 === Infinity`, so a table with a
ratio column and a `maxWidth` of `Infinity` looped forever. Both
`TableOptions.width` and `RenderOptions.maxWidth` are plain numbers with nothing
stopping that value, and a silent hang is worse than the `RangeError` the
arithmetic this replaced would have produced.

The apportionment is now closed-form: a column whose proportional share would
overshoot its cap is granted its want and dropped, its unused cells are reopened
to the rest, and that repeats until everyone still open fits within their share.
One largest-remainder pass then places the cells the shares left as fractions,
so the widths still sum exactly. Each round caps at least one column or is the
last, so the work is bounded by the number of columns.

Rejecting non-finite widths at the boundary would have been the smaller change
and the wrong one: an ordinary table already renders correctly at
`maxWidth: Infinity` — every bounded column caps at its natural width and there
is nothing left to apportion — so a guard would have traded a hang for a
regression. There is a test pinning that case now.

The docblock's claim that one-at-a-time allocation left "no rounding residue for
a second pass to sweep up" stopped being true with this change, so it is gone
rather than left standing next to the second pass.

docs: the narrow-widths ladder labelled a column "width 11" while showing the
width-10 render. A padding level is bought for every column at once or not at
all, so 10, 11 and 12 are one plateau and no width-11 rendering of that example
exists. The ladder now uses widths whose render lands exactly on the request, so
counting characters confirms each label, and says what happens in between.


* fix(table): let a column that wants no cells have none

The seating pass handed every seated column an unconditional first content cell,
and `Math.max(1, ...)` floors in the demand computation made sure no column
could ask for fewer. A zero-width spacer therefore gained a cell it never asked
for: `width: 0` next to a normal column rendered `+---+` where e621b03 rendered
`+--+`.

The floor reached further than a declared width. `_naturalWidth` carried the
same `Math.max(1, ...)`, so a column with no header and no content changed
identically — and a `Table.grid()` used as a gutter is far more likely to take
that path than an explicit `width: 0`.

The seat is now `Math.min(1, want)`. The queue exists to stop one column taking
a second cell before another has its first, and a column that wants nothing has
no place in it; the reservation and apportionment arithmetic that assumed a seat
of 1 is taken net of the seat instead. Spacers pay their divider and padding and
nothing more, which is what they did before the rewrite.

One deliberate difference from e621b03: a negative declared width floors at 0
rather than reaching `" ".repeat(-1)` and throwing. That is the rule #76 already
established for the same class of input, where `normalizePadding` floors every
side at zero as it is parsed.


* fix(table): floor a non-finite width where it enters the layout

`Math.max(0, n)` returns NaN for a NaN input, so a caller's `width: NaN` — a
plausible `total / count` with a zero count — did not merely mis-size its own
column. It reached `budget -= NaN` in the seating pass, and from there every
`budget < cost` comparison was false, because comparisons against NaN always
are. The bounds check was not wrong, it was switched off: every remaining
column got seated regardless of the space, padding and reservations came back
NaN for the whole table, and `" ".repeat(NaN)` renders as `""` rather than
throwing. A two-column table collapsed to `+++` silently.

The same value arrives through three doors — the requested `outerWidth`, a
column's declared `width`, and the `minWidth`/`maxWidth` bounding a natural
width — so it is normalized once at each, rather than guarded at the dozen
comparisons downstream that would otherwise have to survive it.

`n > 0 ? n : 0` rather than `Number.isFinite(n) ? ... : ...`: the comparison
already rejects NaN, since NaN fails every comparison, and it floors negatives
with the same expression it replaces. `Infinity` passes through, which an
unbounded width needs. That is also why a NaN `ratio` needs nothing here —
`distribute` admits a column to its working set on `weight > 0`, which has
excluded NaN all along.

Flooring rather than throwing is the rule already set for out-of-domain numbers
here: #76 floors negative padding as it is parsed, and this branch floors a
negative declared width for the same reason.


* fix(table): measure against the width the container offered

`measure()` laid both ends of its range out against `this.tableWidth ?? maxWidth`,
but `Measurement.get` clamps only the maximum it gets back and passes the
minimum through untouched. A table with a declared width wider than the space it
was being measured in therefore reported a floor computed against the declared
width and a ceiling clamped to the offered one — `{minimum: 13, maximum: 5}` for
three columns measured at `maxWidth: 5`.

That is the same inverted range this method's docblock says is no longer
possible. The claim was true of `outerWidth` and false of the width the caller
actually offered, which is the one the range is read against. Bounding
`outerWidth` by `options.maxWidth` makes it true as written.

The double `_columnDemands()` call goes with it. Both layouts derive from one
array now; the second call only ever recomputed it, and it re-walks every row of
every natural column through `_naturalWidth` to do so — on the entry point
`Layout` and `Columns` hit repeatedly while probing candidate widths.

Scoped to `measure()`. `render()` also lays out at the declared width and does
overflow a narrower container, but e621b03 does that too, so it is long-standing
behaviour of a documented option rather than anything this branch introduced.
Filed as rich-table-width-y1a.


* docs(tables): correct three claims the renderer does not honour

The ladder omitted width 4, and the sentence under it generalizes from the
listed rungs — so "in between it sits on the previous rung" read as a claim
about width 4 that is false: at width 4 only one column is seated, a padding
level therefore costs one cell, and the single leftover cell can afford it.
Width 4 lands exactly on the request and is a rung by the paragraph's own
definition. Listing it makes the existing sentence true for every width from 2
to 16, checked by rendering each one, rather than needing an exception written
beside it. The figure is regenerated from the renderer, which is how the
"width 11" mislabel on this branch was caught.

A declared-`width` column did not "keep its size and its neighbours absorb the
shortfall". Reservations are paid after the frame, the seats and the padding, so
a width too small to cover them shrinks reserved columns too: `width: 5` beside
a natural column renders at one content cell when the table is asked for 8. The
ordering is deliberate — cell priority is `Panel`'s and Python Rich's — so the
claim is corrected to what the renderer does.

Correcting the `expand` row to say it is not wired into sizing left the Grids
section still presenting `Table.grid({ expand: true })` as the way to fill the
terminal. One file said both; the example silently no-ops. It now points at the
sizing note. Wiring `expand` remains rich-table-rrz.

The opening claim is narrowed to a table with no declared `width`, which is the
only shape it holds for: an explicit width overrides a narrower container, and
that is now stated on the option itself.


* fix(padding): floor a non-finite side where padding is parsed

`normalizePadding` floored each side with `Math.max(0, n)`, which returns NaN
unchanged, so its docblock's guarantee — that past this crossing
`" ".repeat(left)` is safe in any renderable without asking what the caller
passed — held for negative sides and not for NaN. `new Table({ padding: NaN })`
collapsed a two-column table to `+++`: `takePerColumn` returned NaN, and
`budget -= per * seated` then made every later bounds check false, since
comparisons against NaN always are.

The floor belongs here rather than at the callsite that found it. Running
`layoutTable`'s destructured sides through the table's own normalizer would
have left `Padding` and `Panel` taking the same NaN through the same door, and
put a second floor for one invariant a layer below the one that already owns it.


* fix(table): keep an infinite bound out of the demand model

`cells()` lets `Infinity` through, which is right where it normalizes the
requested outer width — an unbounded width is deliberate and tested. Reusing it
to build column demands let that value into a model with no room for it:
`UNBOUNDED` is this model's own infinity, and a literal `Infinity` reaching
`distribute` makes a column's weighted share `Infinity / Infinity`, which is
NaN. The NaN then skews every other elastic column, so `minWidth: Infinity`
rendered a 7-cell border above a 9-cell row — the frame broken, not merely one
column mis-sized. `ratio: Infinity` did the same, since both `flexible` and the
elastic branch ask only for `ratio > 0`.

`demandCells` caps at `UNBOUNDED` so a `ColumnDemand` is finite by
construction, and it is applied in all three branches that build one. Mapping
`Infinity` onto `UNBOUNDED` says the intended thing in the vocabulary the model
already has rather than adding a second one.

`distribute`'s `open` filter is deliberately untouched. `weight > 0` is what
has always made a NaN weight harmless, and adding `Number.isFinite` beside it
would guard against a state the constructor no longer produces.

`_naturalWidth` now returns its bounded value unfloored: the floor moved to the
demand it feeds, and keeping both would be two enforcers for one rule.


* test(table): name the NaN-width test after the path it takes

`NaN !== undefined`, so a NaN column `width` takes the declared-width branch and
becomes a declared width of zero — the same demand an explicit `width: 0`
produces. The title claimed it was treated as no declared width, which would
mean falling through to natural sizing and rendering the cell's own content; the
assertion it sits above says otherwise.

The code and `eef1a2f`'s message were already accurate. Only the name
overclaimed, and a name is read as a description of the behaviour whether or not
it is true of it.


* fix(padding): truncate a fractional side where padding is parsed

A cell is not divisible, and `normalizePadding` enforced only the non-negative
half of that domain. A fractional side reached `" ".repeat`, which truncates,
while the box rows around it are measured arithmetically — so `padding: 1.5`
drew 13-cell borders around an 11-cell content row and the frame did not close.

Flooring here rather than at either callsite keeps the guarantee the docblock
already makes: past this crossing a side is a count of cells, so no renderer
downstream has to ask what the caller wrote. `Padding` and `Panel` take the
same crossing and had the same break.


* fix(table): buy whole cells only, whatever width was requested

`cells()` enforced the non-negative half of a cell count's domain and not the
integral half, so a fractional `outerWidth` — `new Table({ width: 10.5 })`, or a
`maxWidth` computed by a caller — left `budget` fractional for the whole layout.
It reached `distribute`'s largest-remainder pass, which tops columns up a whole
cell at a time against a `residue` that was itself fractional, so a residue of
0.5 still bought a full cell. A table asked for 10.5 emitted 11, and 9.5, 7.25
and 3.5 all overshot the same way — the one invariant this branch exists to
hold.

Flooring at the parse point rather than at the top of `distribute` makes that
function's integer assumption true instead of defended, and it is the only place
that catches the same value on its way to the padding and the box rows;
`distribute` is where the overshoot surfaced, not where it entered.

`Infinity` survives `Math.floor`, so the unbounded-width path is unchanged.

fix(panel): divide the requested width once, so no row can overflow it (rich-width-3cf.1) (#76)

* fix(panel): divide the requested width once, so no row can overflow it (rich-width-3cf.1)

`Panel` derived its geometry three times — `panelWidth - 2 - padLeft -
padRight` in `render`, `panelWidth - 2` in each border renderer — and
clamped each derivation differently. At width 1 the unclamped border
subtraction went negative and `String.repeat(-1)` threw `RangeError`.
Between widths 2 and 6 the `Math.max(1, …)` in `render` clamped the
content canvas *up*, so a 2-cell frame enclosed 5-cell content rows,
which the terminal then soft-wrapped, destroying the frame of everything
printed below.

`layoutPanel` now divides the requested width once into fields that sum
to exactly that width, and every row measures from it. Cells go to the
two frame columns, then one cell of content, then the padding, then the
remainder back to content — so content stays visible down to width 3
instead of the panel spending its last cells on padding. Frame columns
are emitted as `box.left.repeat(n)` with n in {0,1}, which needs no
branch because the wire boundary drops zero-length segments.

Content rows now route through `Segment.adjustLineLength`, which crops a
child that rendered wider than its canvas (a `Table` at natural width)
instead of letting it burst the frame, and fills the span in one stroke
— replacing the hand-rolled `rightPad` arithmetic and `_renderBlankLine`,
which is now a content row whose content is nothing.

The test sweeps thirteen panel configurations across widths 1–40 and
asserts every line fits inside the width and no line is ragged.


* fix(panel): keep rendering content at widths that cannot show it

`_renderContent` skipped the wrapped renderable entirely when the canvas
was zero cells, which silently broke the contract the `BorderAccessory`
doc states two dozen lines above it: the thunk form is evaluated after
content has rendered for the current frame, because it reads state that
render populates. At panel width 2 and below the thunk still fired and
read the previous frame.

Content now renders at every width and the geometry decides how many of
its rows survive, so only the row count varies. The nominal width of 1
is a floor `RichText` needs rather than a clamp: its fold walks a cursor
forward by `maxWidth`, so a zero-width canvas spins ~134M iterations and
about a gigabyte before `push` hits the array-length limit — measured,
not inferred. Fixing that loop would delete this floor, but what fold
should emit into a zero-column canvas is a decision for every RichText
caller and belongs with the width sweep in rich-width-3cf.3.

The test asserts the contract where it is observable: an accessory thunk
reading a counter its content renderable increments, at every width from
1 up. It fails against the previous commit at width 1.


* fix(padding): floor padding at zero where it is parsed, once

Negative padding reached the renderers, which handled it three ways:
`Panel` on master drew a 21-cell content row inside a 20-cell border,
`Table` drew a 6-cell row inside a 5-cell border or threw `RangeError:
Invalid count value` depending on how wide the column was, and the
`layoutPanel` geometry introduced by this branch turned the panel case
from silent corruption into a throw. All three are the same defect: the
public `PaddingDimensions` vocabulary admits a value no renderer can
draw.

`normalizePadding` is the crossing between that vocabulary and the
four-sided tuple every renderable indexes by, so the floor goes there
and `" ".repeat(left)` downstream needs no guard in any renderable.

It also existed three times — `padding.ts`, `panel.ts` and `table.ts`,
the latter two byte-identical — so clamping one copy would have left the
bug in the others. There is now one exported parser beside the type it
parses, and the per-renderable defaults stay at their callsites, since
those genuinely differ.

Both tests were checked against the unfixed code. The Table one earns
its keep twice: written first as `not.toThrow`, it passed on master's
corrupt output, because that input draws a ragged table rather than
throwing. Asserting the table is a rectangle catches both shapes.


* fix(panel): measure against the same division the panel renders against

`measure()` and `_getPanelWidth()` still derived the content budget as
`Math.max(1, maxWidth - 2 - padLeft - padRight)`. Before `layoutPanel`
existed that formula was textually identical to the one in `render`, so
the two could not disagree; introducing the geometry made them two
sources for one fact that diverge exactly in the 0-2 band this branch
was written for — the geometry gives 0 content cells there, the formula
insists on 1. The comment on `PanelGeometry` claiming one authoritative
division was written eight lines above the code contradicting it.

Both now read the geometry. Taking the frame overhead from it as well,
rather than the constant `2 + padLeft + padRight`, fixes a second
incoherence with the same cause — a panel does not spend cells on a
right frame column or padding it cannot afford, so counting them
produced a measurement whose minimum exceeded its own maximum:

  before: @1 {minimum: 5, maximum: 1}   after: @1 {1, 1}
          @2 {minimum: 5, maximum: 2}           @2 {2, 2}
          @20 {minimum: 9, maximum: 15}         @20 {9, 15}

The negative-padding tests asserted the rendered lines were rectangular,
which `layoutPanel` guarantees for any non-negative clamp — they would
have passed had the floor been `Math.abs`. They now compare against the
`padding: 0` render, which is the claim their names make. Verified by
mutating the clamp to `Math.abs` and watching both fail.

test(seam): make host access a checked list, not four claims (rich-seam-981.6) (#75)

* test(seam): make host access a checked list, not four claims (rich-seam-981.6)

Four comments claimed who owns node TTY access and no two agreed on the
scope. `docs/widgets.md` said `NodeTerminalHost` "is the only thing that
touches `process.stdin` and `process.stdout`" — false; `src/node/prompt.ts`
reads both. The three in `src/` survived only by narrowing until they no
longer overlapped their counterexamples, and none of the four mentioned
`prompt.ts` at all, because none of them was checked.

`HOST_ACCESS` in `test/seam/ambient-process.ts` is now the one home: every
file in `src/` that reads the ambient `process`, the property names it takes,
and a required `why`. The gate fails when a file joins the list without an
entry and when an entry outlives the read it was granted for. Granularity is
per-property on purpose — it is what let the scan answer the question the
narrowed sentences were circling, and answer it against them: there is no
sole reader of `process.stdin`, there are two, and what is true is that both
sit behind `package.json#exports` subpaths.

Not the browser-safety rule next door, though both scan for the same
identifier. That one asks whether a module-scope read throws when a browser
evaluates the barrel; this one asks what the package takes off the host in
any scope. A function-body leak passes there and fails here — pinned from
both sides by a fixture in each suite. `isNameSlot` moves to
`test/seam/identifiers.ts` so the two rules share it rather than drift.

The prose now points at the list instead of restating it.


* fix(seam): prune type queries as a subtree, not by parent kind

`type T = typeof process.env` reported a whole-object host read. The
identifier's parent there is the `QualifiedName`, not the `TypeQueryNode`,
so matching on the parent saw nothing — while the function's own doc
comment promised a `typeof` takes nothing off the host. Pruning the query's
subtree covers every spelling of it at once and retires the parent-kind
clause; type positions are otherwise still walked, which is the deliberate
difference from `browser-safe.ts`.

`docs/widgets.md` stops naming the two stream members. A published page is
the wrong place to send a reader into `test/seam/`, but enumerating what
`HOST_ACCESS` enumerates is the drift this PR exists to remove — so the
member list goes and the claims that remain are ones the suite pins.

test(seam): forbid upward imports out of core (rich-seam-981.5) (#74)

* test(seam): forbid upward imports out of core (rich-seam-981.5)

CLAUDE.md claimed `src/core/` has no upward calls and told the reader to
verify it with a grep. The grep in that section — `from "\./[a-z]+\.js"` —
matched same-directory imports only, so it could not have found either of
the two edges that actually leave core. A reader following the instruction
got a clean result from a check incapable of returning anything else.

`test/seam/layering.test.ts` replaces it: walk every file under `src/core/`,
resolve every import, fail naming file, line and specifier when an edge
leaves the layer without a sanction — and fail the other way too, when a
sanction outlives the import it permitted, so the exemption list cannot
accumulate permissions nobody needs.

The rule counts type-only imports, deliberately. `browser-safe.ts` skips
erased edges because a browser cannot trip over one; a layer can, because
`import type { Panel } from "../renderables/"` is core knowing the shape of
renderables. Rather than a flag selecting between two collectors, or a
second traversal making one fact into two maps, `moduleSpecifiers` now tags
each edge with `erased` and `runtimeModuleSpecifiers` derives by filtering.

The two sanctioned edges (`color.ts -> themes/palette.ts`,
`console.ts -> renderables/rule.ts`) are kept, as CLAUDE.md already records
them. `Console.rule()` stays — it is documented and tested — but the
duplicate `RuleOptions` that `console.ts` declared beside `rule.ts`'s is
gone, along with the field-by-field forwarding that existed only to bridge
the two copies.

Every rule was falsified against real source: a runtime upward import, a
type-only upward import, a removed sanctioned edge, and a blinded collector
each turn exactly the intended gate red.


* test(seam): verify the sanctioned edges close no cycle

Three review findings, all valid.

Every `why` on a sanctioned edge argued the same safety property in its own
words — the edge points up, but it closes no module-level cycle — and
nothing re-read those words. A gate whose exemptions rest on unverified
claims is the exact shape this file was written to retire, so the fix is to
check the property rather than to stop advertising it.

`cyclicSanctionedEdges` asks it generically: for each sanctioned edge, the
runtime walk from the target must not reach the source. Deliberately a
*module* cycle rather than a layer one, because the two edges are safe for
different reasons and only this question covers both — `themes/palette.ts`
never returns to core at runtime, while `renderables/rule.ts` imports four
core primitives and is safe because none reaches `core/console.ts`. A
reciprocal "the import back must stay type-only" rule would have been wrong
about the second edge and right about the first by coincidence.

`isInside` was a second implementation of the four-part path-containment
idiom `isUnderSrc` already had, comment and all. Both now call one
`isPathInside`, so hardening it cannot leave one caller behind in the
string-prefix bug the layering test pins.

The CLAUDE.md sentence claiming the removed grep matched same-directory
imports only was false: the pattern actually removed was
`from "\.\.?/[a-z/]+\.js"`, which matches `../` and would have found both
edges. That was PR #66's pattern, corrected in this file long before this
branch, and the sentence is rewritten to attribute it and to give the real
argument for a gate over a working grep — a grep judges no sanction and
cannot see an exemption that outlived its import.

Both new rules falsified against real source: a runtime import added from
palette.ts back to color.ts turns the cycle gate red alone, and reinstating
the string-prefix bug in the shared helper turns the sibling-directory test
red.


* test(seam): compare paths in one canonical spelling

Three review findings, all valid.

The layering rules compared `path.relative` output against forward-slash
literals with `===`. That holds on POSIX and fails on every Windows host,
where `src\core\console.ts` never equals `src/core/console.ts` — so the gate
would report both sanctioned edges as simultaneously unsanctioned and stale,
accusing untouched code of exactly what it exists to catch. Four sites had
the exposure; `browser-safe.ts` next door computes the same paths but only
ever renders them, which is why this arrived with this branch.

Fixed at the representation rather than at the comparisons: `repoRelative`
in `test/coverage/extract.ts` is now the single crossing where an OS path
becomes the spelling the suite compares on. Normalizing at each comparison
would have left the fifth site to be forgotten.

Its test is pinned but honest — on a POSIX host the assertion holds with or
without the canonicalization, so it gates only on Windows and the comment
says so. Green on this CI is not evidence the normalization survived, and
recording that is better than implying a check stronger than the one there.

The transitive-cycle fixture carried a comment left over from an earlier
draft, naming rule.ts and console.ts while the fixture used color.ts and
panel.ts. Replaced with the chain it actually walks — panel.ts reaches
color.ts through core/style.ts — and shorter than the wrong version, since
the repair is to say the true thing once.

CLAUDE.md described the gate as failing two ways when it now fails three,
omitting the cycle check — which is the one that makes the safety claims in
the bullets directly above it verified rather than asserted. A reader
checking whether anything backs those claims would have concluded nothing
did.


* docs(seam): give each sanctioned edge's reason one home

CLAUDE.md claimed the cycle gate holds "each bullet above to its safety
argument", but only the first bullet carried one — the second named the
edge and stopped. The two renderings of the sanctioned pair diverged in
content, not just in form, so a reader of CLAUDE.md alone had nothing to
hold the second edge to.

Fixed by subtracting rather than by mirroring. Writing the reason into both
files would satisfy one-source-of-truth in form and violate it in substance:
two copies that agree today and are free to drift. That is not hypothetical
for this particular sentence — this ticket's own description asserted the
type-only direction backwards, claiming core→themes was the erased edge when
it is the runtime one, which is the same reasoning going wrong in a third
location.

So CLAUDE.md now names the two edges, states the property they share (each
points up without closing a runtime cycle) once, and points at the required
`why` field as the single home for the per-edge argument. Nothing was lost:
the palette type-only reasoning still exists, in the one place that sits
beside the gate keeping it true.

Two cross-references in layering.ts cited CLAUDE.md for text that just
moved; both now point at `why`.


* test(seam): ask erasure in both directions of a sanctioned cycle

`cyclicSanctionedEdges` was named for cycles and computed reachability. It
asked only whether the target loads its way back to the source, never
whether the sanctioned edge itself is a runtime edge — so a sanction spelled
`import type` would have been reported as closing a runtime cycle even
though it loads no module and cannot participate in one. Both current
entries are runtime edges forward, which is a fact about today's list rather
than a property of the type, so the gap was latent rather than absent.

A cycle needs a runtime edge at every step. Backwards that is
`reachableSourceModules`, which already walks runtime edges only; forwards
it is now an explicit condition on the observed import. The information
needed no new plumbing — `OutboundEdge.erased` already carried it, and the
function takes `(edges, layer)` like `unsanctioned` and `unexercised`, where
it was previously the odd one out.

A sanction matching no import falls out as not-cyclic, leaving the staleness
arm to report it once instead of two gates reporting one fault.

Pinned with a paired fixture: the same `color.ts -> panel.ts` edge, runtime
and type-only, differing in nothing but `erased`, asserted to opposite
outcomes. Dropping the new condition turns the type-only arm and the
no-matching-import arm red while both original cycle arms stay green, so the
narrowing is additive rather than a weakening of what the gate detected.


* docs(seam): state what isPathInside actually guarantees

The helper's doc claimed `path.relative` "absorbs OS separator differences
and symlink/realpath variation". The first half is true; the second is not —
`path.relative` is lexical and never reads the filesystem, so a symlink and
its target compare as unrelated paths.

The sentence predates this branch; `isUnderSrc` carried it privately. What
changed is that extracting the shared helper promoted it into a documented
contract, which is the reason to fix it rather than leave it.

The code is unchanged and correct: every path either caller sees derives
from `REPO_ROOT` — the file walk is rooted there and module resolution runs
against what it reached — so both sides always share one spelling. Adding
`realpathSync` would put filesystem I/O in a pure comparison to defend
against a mixture no current caller can produce. The doc now says that, and
names the obligation it leaves for a future caller holding paths from two
sources.

test(seam): fail the unit suite when the barrel stops being browser-safe (rich-seam-981.4) (#73)

* test(seam): fail the unit suite when the barrel stops being browser-safe (rich-seam-981.4)

The browser-safe barrel was a claim in README.md and CLAUDE.md plus a grep
someone ran by hand and pasted into a ticket. The only automated guard was
indirect — vite bundles examples/, Playwright boots them in Chromium — which
catches a leak after a full docs build and a browser install, and reports it
as "a demo failed to boot" rather than naming the import.

test/seam/graph.ts walks the runtime import graph from a set of roots,
bounded to src/, carrying the chain that reached each module. It needs no
ts.Program: reachability is syntactic, and an `import type` edge is erased
before the module runs, so it is not an edge. A relative specifier that
fails to resolve throws rather than silently shrinking the graph.

test/seam/browser-safe.ts is the rule, pure over one parsed file: a `node:*`
specifier on an edge that survives to runtime, or a read of ambient
`process`/`Buffer` at module scope. Module scope is the line — color.ts and
console.ts both read `process` from inside a function body, where the read
happens only if a caller asks for it. There is no exemption for a module-scope
`typeof process` guard: nothing needs one, and the fix is always a function.

Roots come from package.json#exports minus src/node/, so a new subpath is
covered the moment it lands. loadCompilerOptions and isUnderSrc are now
exported from the coverage verifier rather than restated here.

Falsified both halves rather than trusting a green check. Adding
`import { readFileSync } from "node:fs"` to src/core/segment.ts fails with
`src/core/segment.ts:1 — imports "node:fs" / reached by: src/index.ts →
src/core/segment.ts`; adding `import "../node/save.js"` instead fails with
the three-hop chain through the airlock. The scanner's own shapes — type-only
imports, function bodies, class field initializers, name slots vs reads — are
pinned by fixtures.

CLAUDE.md's browser-safe section said the failure "does not land on the person
who wrote the import". That is no longer true, so it now says what does.


* test(seam): close the scanner's blind spots and false positives

Six holes, all found by review, four of them shapes the module's own
comment claimed it did not have.

A Node builtin imported without the `node:` prefix — `from "fs"` — type
checks here, resolves outside src/ so the walk skips it, and matched no
rule. `builtinModules` from the running Node now backs the check; it
already carries the slashed forms, so membership is one lookup.

Deferred execution was two half-truths. A function body was pruned even
when the function is immediately invoked, so `(() => process.env)()` at
module scope read nothing; parameter defaults were not pruned at all, so
`function ask(out = process.stdout) {}` reported a read that only happens
on a call. Both are the same question — does this wait for someone to call
the function — so they are now one predicate, which is what makes
`(function (o = process.stdout) {})()` come out right where two carve-outs
would each have missed the other's exception.

`ambient` meant *spelled* `process`, so a module declaring or importing its
own binding of that name failed a gate about Node globals. It now means
spelled `process` and bound nowhere in this module, collected from
`sf.statements` — no checker, no scope walk. A binding inside a
module-scope block still reports; that is the safe direction.

`const { process: local } = config` named a property of `config` and was
read as the global. `BindingElement.propertyName` is a name slot.

The `ShorthandPropertyAssignment` carve-out was the one branch in
`isNameSlot` written to make something fire and the one with no test that
it fires. It has one now.

CLAUDE.md's new paragraph restated this module's header nearly verbatim —
the two-descriptions-of-one-surface trap the file warns about thirty lines
earlier, added by the commit whose purpose was fixing an instance of it. It
is now the pointer it should have been, and shorter than what it replaced.


* test(seam): erasure, shadowing and heritage were each half a rule

Ten findings, and three of them were the round-1 fixes having bought their
own defects.

Erasure was read at the declaration only. `import { type Stats } from
"node:fs"` leaves `importClause.isTypeOnly` false — verified, not assumed —
so the per-specifier form `isolatedModules` encourages reported a specifier
that never survives. The question is now whether anything in the statement
survives: a default or namespace binding survives whatever the braces say,
a side-effect import has nothing to erase, and a named list erases only
when every element carries its own modifier.

Shadowing counted type-space declarations. `interface Buffer {}` shadows
the type and leaves the value where it was, so it suppressed a genuine
read — a false negative, bought by the fix for a false positive, in the
direction this file calls the worse one. Interfaces and type aliases are
out; so are type-only imports and specifiers, which bind nothing to shadow
with.

`ts.isTypeNode` calls a class `extends` clause a type node. It is an
expression that evaluates to the superclass the instant the declaration
runs, so the blanket prune hid `class Host extends Buffer {}` entirely. An
interface's `extends` produces the same node under the same token and *is*
erased, so the carve-out asks the heritage clause's parent as well.

An export specifier's local reference is `propertyName ?? name`, and it is
local only without a `from` clause — one rule, because the two spellings
pull opposite ways: `export { process }` reads the binding, `export
{ process } from "./m.js"` does not. Elsewhere a `propertyName` names a
slot in another table — an object's property, another module's export —
which covers the renamed import the same way.

A constructor is never the callee; its class is. `new (class {
constructor(o = process.stdout) {} })()` deferred a parameter default that
runs on load.

`global` joins the ambient list: Node-only, no browser counterpart, and
unlike the CommonJS names it has no backstop in an ESM package.

CLAUDE.md said "its header comment" of a paragraph naming only the test
file, while the rationale lives in the implementation file. Named it.


* test(seam): one deferral rule, three triggers

Three findings, and the useful one is that the deferral rule was right in
substance and applied to only one of the three places it belongs.

A function's body waits for a call. So does a constructor's — via its class.
An instance field waits for construction, and an accessor body waits for a
property read. All four are the same question, and the scan was answering it
for two of them: an instance field initializer was flagged even though
importing the module never runs it, which contradicted the constructor body
directly above it that the same file already deferred.

So `isDeferred` asks it once, and `isImmediatelyRun` picks the trigger.
`isImmediatelyRead` is `isImmediatelyInvoked` with the other syntax, sharing
the parenthesis walk. An accessor consults the read trigger because it has no
callable form — asking it the call question would always answer no, which is
what hid `{ get w() { return process.env } }.w`.

Static fields and `static {}` blocks wait for nothing; they run with the
declaration and are not pruned. The static block already worked, because
`ts.isFunctionLike` excludes it — now by fixture rather than by luck.

The header said the ambient rule fires on `process` or `Buffer` while
`AMBIENT_GLOBALS` held three names, stale from the commit that added the
third. It now names the constant, so the list has one home and the sentence
cannot disagree with it.

Two findings were declined on evidence rather than argument. `import {} from
"node:fs"` is not preserved by the emitter: compiled under this repo's
settings in an ESM package, it and `export {} from "node:os"` and
`import { type Stats }` all vanish, leaving only the unrelated export — so
treating an empty named clause as erased is what the emitter does. And
`export * as process from "./m.js"` binds nothing locally; tsc answers a
later `process.env` with "Cannot find name 'process'", having gone looking
for the global, so flagging it is correct and collecting the name would buy
back the false negative the interface finding just removed.


* test(seam): the trigger is one notion, not a branch per shape

Two findings asked for a branch each — a getter reached through
`new (…)().w`, a method through `(…).m()`. Taking them that way is an
enumeration with no cap, because consumption chains compose and the next
report would be `new (…)().m()`.

The closed version underneath is one notion: the container's value — the
object or class as written, or what `new` makes of it — is consumed right
here. Asked of the four function-like member kinds, which is an enumeration
that ends. A plain function is its own container and is consumed by a call;
a constructor's class by `new`; an accessor by a property read; a method by
that read being called. Neither an accessor nor a method has a callable form
of its own, so asking either the plain-call question could only ever answer
no — the same reason the getter case failed before.

Pruning a whole `PropertyDeclaration` hid its computed name, which runs when
the class body does whether or not the member is static. Only the initializer
is deferred now, which is both narrower and correct, and brings decorators
along for free. The parameter branch legitimately differs: a parameter name
can never be an expression, so pruning the whole parameter is safe there.

`export { type process }` referenced nothing at runtime and was read as a
live local reference — the import side of that question was already asked in
graph.ts.

`resolveEdge`'s throw is the walk's guard against silently narrowing the
graph, and nothing in a healthy `src/` had ever made it fire: the one line
whose regression would look exactly like success. It is exported and pinned,
with the null arm pinned beside it, rather than tested through a broken
fixture on disk that `tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` would reject.

Each new rule was falsified against its own fixture: neutering the method
trigger and the `new` unwrapping fails exactly the consumed-on-the-spot
test, restoring the coarse property prune fails exactly the class test, and
narrowing the throw fails exactly the resolve test.


* docs: leave the ambient-globals list one home

Last round I stopped `browser-safe.ts`'s header from enumerating
AMBIENT_GLOBALS, on the grounds that a list written twice is a list that
will disagree with itself — and in the same commit edited a sentence in
CLAUDE.md that was enumerating it, without noticing it was the same shape.
That sentence now names the constant too.

Fourth instance of one defect in this PR: prose beside code, made stale by
the commit that changed the code. The general form, which is what the next
sweep should look for: when prose enumerates something the code also
enumerates, point at the code's copy instead. Grepping for the changed
symbol never finds these — none of the four named one.

feat(console): take the host environment by injection (rich-seam-981.3) (#72)

* feat(console): take the host environment by injection (rich-seam-981.3)

exactly one read of the ambient global in the module.
