feat(traceback): install behind the node seam and cover rejections (rich-seam-981.1) (#70)

* feat(traceback): install behind the node seam and cover rejections (rich-seam-981.1)

`Traceback.install` called `process.on` and `process.exit` from
`src/renderables/`, reachable from the main barrel. It was lazy, so a browser
import did not throw — the browser-safe guarantee held by care rather than by
construction. The installer now lives in `src/node/traceback.ts` behind a
`./node/traceback` subpath; the `Traceback` renderable is pure rendering and
stays in the barrel, which no longer references `process` at all.

The installer also handles `unhandledRejection`. A promise-based library that
pretty-printed only synchronous crashes covered half the failure surface. Both
channels run one `report` pipeline; a rejection's `unknown` reason crosses a
`toError` checkpoint first, which names non-`Error` reasons
`UnhandledRejection` and clears the synthesized stack rather than reporting
rich-js's own frames as the fault site.

Fixes a truncation defect carried over from the old installer: `process.exit(1)`
immediately after writing cuts a piped stderr at the pipe buffer. Measured on a
549,973-byte traceback through a pipe — 65,536 bytes arrived, 88% lost, exactly
where a crash report matters most. The installer now exits from the write's
drain callback; the same measurement delivers all 549,973 bytes.

BREAKING: `Traceback.install` is removed. Use `installTraceback` from
`@promptctl/rich-js/node/traceback`. Folded into the unpublished 0.8.0 rather
than minting a version with no released predecessor to diff against.

Verified: all six behaviours falsified by source mutation with known-good
baseline and restored runs; real child-process crashes for both channels render
through Traceback and exit 1; coverage gate confirmed to see the new subpath by
observing it fail when the demo drops the import; lint, 1782 tests, docs:build
and demos:build green.


* fix(traceback): trust neither crash payload to be an Error; one handler per process

`@types/node` annotates the `uncaughtException` payload as `Error`, and I
reasoned from the annotation. It is not a runtime guarantee — `throw "boom"`
delivers the raw string, and the renderable then read `.name` and `.message`
off it as `undefined`, reporting a bare "Error: " and discarding the one detail
a crash report exists to carry. Both channels now register the same `report`
function, which takes `unknown` and crosses the `toError` checkpoint itself, so
a raw payload cannot reach `Traceback` at all rather than merely being
unlikely to. That removes the two adapter closures as well: the file's claim
that both channels are one pipeline is now literally true.

`toError` names non-`Error` payloads `NonError`; `UnhandledRejection` became a
lie the moment the same checkpoint also covered `throw`.

`installTraceback` replaces its handler instead of appending one. Three calls
registered three listeners, so a single crash rendered three times with three
`process.exit(1)` sequences racing. Last call wins, options included — the
alternatives both have a bad arm: throwing takes an app down at startup for a
benign reason, and no-op-on-second silently discards the second call's options.
The registry gets a single owner holding the installed handler, initialized to
a no-op rather than null so removal needs no first-call branch.

Docs stop showcasing `showLocals`, which is accepted, stored, and never read
by `render()`. That gap is older and wider than this PR — `docs/traceback.md`
has carried an ASCII "locals" panel documenting output the library has never
emitted — and is filed as rich-traceback-i5d rather than expanded into here;
JS cannot introspect frame locals from `error.stack`, so closing it is a design
decision about an inspector seam, not a review fix.

Declined the suggested 2s force-exit fallback on the stderr drain. Measured:
node's own default crash handler hangs identically on a stalled consumer, so
the hang is POSIX backpressure rather than anything this change introduced,
and a deadline would put every consumer slower than 2s back into silent
truncation — trading a visible hang for invisible data loss. Reasoning is on
the PR thread.

Verified: both fixes falsified by source mutation with known-good baseline and
restored runs; real child processes confirm `NonError: 'raw string boom'` and a
triple install reporting one crash once; lint, 1784 tests, docs:build green.


* fix(traceback): latch the first crash, and keep frames from other realms

A cascade — cleanup rejecting a promise while the first report is still
draining — started a second write and a second `process.exit(1)`, and whichever
drained first cut the other off mid-frame. Reproduced with two ~1500-frame
tracebacks through a pipe: both headers present, output ending "  deep
file:///", a frame severed mid-path. That is the same silent truncation this
branch already argued against on the drain-timeout thread, reached by a
different route. `report` now latches: the first crash is the fault, the rest
is its wake, and one complete report of the fault beats two corrupt ones — the
same thing node does, where a default handler dies on the first fatal error and
never reports the cascade. The latch is a closure per install, not a module
global, so it cannot leak across installs.

`toError` gated on `instanceof Error`, which is realm-dependent. An error
thrown inside a `node:vm` context is a real error with real frames but a
foreign prototype, so its frames were discarded by the one component that
exists to show them — a regression against the old installer, which passed the
payload straight through. The gate is now `util.types.isNativeError`, which
reads V8's internal error slot and is realm-independent; it is a real predicate
rather than a heuristic, and needs no cast. Values it correctly rejects keep
any `stack` string they carry, so a duck-typed thrower still renders its
frames while being named honestly.

Two comments claimed more than the code delivers. The console comment said
stderr drove colour depth and width; `getTerminalSize` reads only
`process.stdout.columns`, so a stderr crash report wraps at stdout's width.
Comment corrected and narrowed, exception filed as rich-console-ujo. The demo
comment claimed the handler was installed "before anything can throw"; ESM
evaluates a module's imports before its body, so the guarantee is "before
`run`". The docs tip carried the same false premise while advising a placement
that cannot deliver it, and now explains the constraint and the two placements
that do work.

One of this round's tests was wrong before it was right: the duck-typed-stack
fixture asserted a filename that `inspect` already places in the message, so it
passed with the stack discarded. It now asserts a parsed frame's rendering,
which nothing but a preserved stack can produce.

Verified: every fix falsified by source mutation with known-good baseline and
restored runs; real processes confirm the race repro now reports one crash
ending on a complete frame, and a vm-context error rendering as
"Error: from another realm" at evalmachine.<anonymous>:1; lint, 1787 tests,
docs:build green.


* docs(traceback): drop the frames claim that stack salvage made false

The sentence promised a NonError payload renders with no frames. Adding
`stackOf` in 3bcc8a4 made that false for a duck-typed thrower carrying its own
stack. Deleting the clause rather than qualifying it: a qualifier is one more
claim to keep true the next time `toError` changes, and what frames appear is
something the output already answers.

feat(coverage): hold types to reachability, values to demos (rich-coverage-0as.1) (#69)

The demo-coverage gate asked every public export one question — "is this
name in an import statement under examples/?" — and 74 of the 102 exports

decides which evidence counts — once, where the universe is partitioned,
not branched through the invariants. A value is demonstrated by a demo
naming it. A type is demonstrated by `collectTypeClosure`: reachable
through type positions from a demonstrated value, which is exactly the
condition under which changing it breaks `examples/`. The type check is
derived from the value check rather than parallel to it — demonstrate the
class and its options type follows.

The gate section still described one question asked of every export and an

* fix(demo): both exporters drain one recording buffer; label the API break

`exportText` and `exportHtml` both default `clear: true` and both read
`Console._recorded`, so the dual-export path added in the previous commit
wrote the second file from an already-emptied buffer — silently, exit 0.
Verified by reverting the fix: EXPORT_TEXT landed at 0 bytes.

keeps the loop position-independent; nothing needs the buffer cleared
because the process exits immediately after.

without a version signal would ship a break under a patch. Bumped to
0.8.0 — pre-1.0 semver's breaking-change slot — via the
`npm version minor --no-git-tag-version` step publish.yml documents.

Three comment counts dropped rather than corrected: "(all 17)" box
variants, "four members" on WidgetBase's abstracts, and EXPORT_HTML named
as the recording trigger. A count beside the list it counts is a second
representation of one fact and rots on the next addition; naming the
members and deferring the env-var list to the bootstrap cannot.


* fix(coverage): private members and erased imports must not launder evidence

Two ways the floor could be satisfied by something no consumer can reach.

`collectTypeClosure` walked the whole declaration subtree of a demonstrated
value, so a type named only in a `private` member counted as reachable —
a surface nothing outside the class can touch. The walk now skips class
elements marked `private` or named with `#`.

`visitImports` did not read `isTypeOnly`. The checker resolves
`import type { SomeClass }` to the same SymbolFlags.Value symbol as a value
import, so an import erased before the demo runs satisfied a check that
asks whether a demo can name what it runs. Both the clause form and the
per-specifier form are now skipped.

Neither gap was hiding a live false pass — the suite is green without any
allowlist change — so both were confirmed by falsification instead:
`KeyEvent` rebound as `import type` is reported an undemonstrated value,
and a probe type reachable only through a private method is reported an
undemonstrated type.

Also corrects the claim in collectTypeClosure's doc comment. It said a type
reached this way is one "the demo's own compilation depends on, so changing
it breaks examples/", which is false — for a type on an uncalled public
method, changing it breaks only its own module, which assertProgramClean
already covers. What the walk establishes is weaker and worth stating
plainly: the type is on the public surface of a value a demo runs.


* fix(coverage): a declaration's surface is its signature, not its body

Two findings, one rule. `visitTypePositions` had no case for
`import("m").T`, so `TerminalTheme`'s public `palette:
import("../themes/palette.js").Palette` parameter was surface the walk
stepped over. And `forEachChild` descended into member bodies and
initializers, so a type named in a local annotation or a cast inside a
called method counted as surface — contradicting the docstring rewritten
last round to stop overclaiming.

Both ask the same question: which positions in a declaration are its type
surface? Answering it twice would give the walk two rules to drift
between, so `isOffSurface` states it once — prune private members, bodies
and initializers; everything else is signature. Pruning rather than
enumerating the positions that count, because a missed declaration kind
fails silently in the direction that marks a type reachable when it is not.

The body pruning has two live instances, which the review could not name:
`PrintOptions` and `ThemePaletteData` were reachable only through
implementation. Both are now allowlisted with the real cause. `print`
takes `...args: unknown[]` and sniffs its options off the last argument,
so no signature carries the type; `THEMES` is unannotated so
`ThemeName = keyof typeof THEMES` stays a literal union. Neither is
worth reshaping src/ to satisfy a gate.

Adds test/coverage/extract.test.ts. Every gap in this walk so far was
found by review, not by a test, because its only exercise was one
aggregate pass over the real tree that reports pass or fail and cannot
say which position was mishandled. The walk is pure over an AST, so nine
fixtures pin it with no Program and no checker. Each fix was falsified
against them: dropping the import-type case fails one, dropping the
body pruning fails two, dropping the private-member exclusion from last
round fails one.

"went from 102 entries to one" was true when written and false three
commits later, once the body-pruning fix surfaced PrintOptions and
ThemePaletteData and this PR added them. Rotting after shipping is the
worse failure — nobody touched the sentence.

Fourth count-in-prose to rot here: "(all 17)" box variants, "except four
members" over a list of five, "102 exports" where 74 were the relevant
ones, and this. Each was a number beside the thing it counts with nothing
keeping them in step, so writing "three" would buy one entry of accuracy
and re-arm the trap. The 102 stays — fixed history, and the evidence for
why the split exists. The live count is replaced by what it stood for:
an entry claims no demo can reach the export, and making that claim is
the big deal, whatever the cardinality. `grep` answers the rest, and the
next paragraph already points at it.


* fix(coverage): a function-like initializer is signature, not implementation

`export const f = (x: A): B => {...}` declares A and B on the arrow, and
the arrow is the variable's initializer — so pruning initializers wholesale
threw the whole signature away. Both fixtures returned [] before the fix.
`isBodyOrInitializer` now descends into a function-like node; the
body rule above it prunes the body one level down, so nested arrows that
are genuinely an enclosing function's body stay pruned.

The fixtures went in first and were confirmed failing before the fix. That
order is the point: extract.test.ts was added last round so the next gap in
this walk would be caught by a test, and it was not — every fixture
declared its types on class members, so the tests pinned the rule I had in
mind rather than the surface the walk has to handle. Two of the eleven now
cover arrow-const and class-field-arrow.

Also removes two enumerations rather than correcting them. The dropdown
demo described `Placement` as a two-member union when it has three
(`inline` is live, switched on in screen.ts), and coverage-allowlist.ts's
own header said "It carries one" directly above three entries — the same
count-in-prose fixed in CLAUDE.md one commit earlier and not here, across
the shortest possible distance for a fact to drift. Both now say what the
thing is instead of how many there are.

feat(color)!: colors are values — delete the spec grammar and name families (v0.7.0) (#57)

* feat(color)!: colors are values; delete the spec grammar and name families

A color could not survive between two operations — every color function
resolved and applied in one breath — so composing two color operations had to
be spelled as a string grammar ("primary-darken-3 50%"), which is function
application with the calls written as punctuation. Every new color operation
needed a new grammar production, and the grammar could only ever modify colors
already registered in a palette.

A color now crosses the template seam as a #RRGGBB string, so it holds in a
$var, passes between operations, and composes by nesting. The simple case is a
literal prefix of the composed case, so an author adds an adjustment by
wrapping working code rather than rewriting it into a different form.

Added:
- themes/colorRef.ts — resolveColorRef/parseHexColor, the ONE checkpoint from
  an author-written reference (palette name or hex) to a ColorRgba. Idempotent
  on hex, so callers never branch on "name or already a color".
- template-bindings/color-funcs.ts — colorFuncs(): darken, lighten, mix,
  contrastOn, readableOn, and one function per ThemeKey OKLCH axis, derived
  from the axis set so the table is compiler-proven total. Palette-free: a
  consumer with no theme system gets the whole vocabulary from hex literals.
- fg/bg as the only two color sinks, taking the color as an argument.

Deleted:
- PaletteResolver and its modifier/alpha/auto grammar. With the grammar gone
  the class was Palette.get plus hex parsing, and it had zero other callers.
- palette, paletteOver, auto, hex, rgb, color(256-index), on, the 16 ANSI
  name appliers, and the generated per-palette-variable appliers. A themed
  palette carries ~150 variables of which ~14 are legal template identifiers,
  so that name family reached under a tenth of its own domain and the rest
  needed a different expression shape for the same intent.

paletteFuncs now takes `() => Palette` and registers exactly one function,
`color`. A captured palette froze template bodies to whichever theme was
current at engine construction while the rest of a consumer's colors moved on
— two palettes in one render. The getter costs nothing structurally: FuncMap
bodies run at evaluate time, so parse-once/evaluate-many is untouched.

readableOn takes its WCAG ratio explicitly rather than defaulting to 4.5: the
threshold is the decision the function makes, and a caller muting text on
purpose would be silently un-muted by an implicit AA floor.

Also derives foreground-muted/background-muted in buildPalette, and adds a
numeric-argument gate so an under-supplied call reports the missing argument
instead of surfacing as a NaN RGB channel three layers away.

fix(strip): PowerlineJoiner join is structural, not bg-decided (0.5.2) (#54)

* fix(strip): PowerlineJoiner join is structural, not bg-decided (bump 0.5.0)

The mid-join early-returned EMPTY when adjacent edge bgs matched, making
background colour decide whether a join cell exists at all — paint
masquerading as structure ([LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow]). A join now
exists between every pair of items unconditionally; the chevron is painted
from the two edge bgs and is simply invisible when they are equal. A same-bg
seam between two distinct items survives as a real boundary, and an
item-aware consumer (one segment = one strip item) never relies on the
joiner to coalesce an item's interior.

Rewrites the same-bg test block to assert the structural join + invisible
paint instead of suppression; drops the now-unused SGR-count test.

* fix(strip): no left bg → no separator; unify PowerlineJoiner positions (0.5.1)

A no-bg edge made the always-emit join paint a glyph in the terminal's
default styling — a visible stray arrow between fg-only items, where the
previous code returned EMPTY. The separator is painted in the LEFT edge's
bg (the colour bleeding rightward); with no left bg there is nothing to
paint, so there is no separator.

Collapses the start-cap / mid-join / end-cap branches into one expression:
the endpoints are the DATA cases where a neighbour's bg is absent (no left
bg ⇒ EMPTY, the start cap; no right bg ⇒ bleed out, the end cap), not
control-flow special cases. Equal REAL bgs still emit (invisible, present)
— a same-bg seam between two items stays a structural boundary.

Adds tests: fg-only items emit no separator anywhere; a left item with a bg
still bleeds into a right item without one.

* fix(strip): treat terminal-default bg as no-paint (close enumeration gap) (0.5.2)

The no-bg gate matched only `undefined`, missing the equivalent representation:
an explicit terminal-DEFAULT bgcolor (`Style.parse('… on default')`, isDefault
=== true) is a real ColorSpec but renders as the terminal background — transparent,
nothing to paint. It slipped past the gate and emitted a separator bleeding the
'default' colour. paintableBg folds both 'undefined' and 'isDefault' to one
'no colour' case, so the gate cannot be fooled by an explicit on-default bg.

Also corrects the test-suite header comment (the middle join is no longer
'UNCONDITIONAL' — absence of a left colour elides it) and adds an on-default test.

feat(strip): collapse StripCell into RichText; edge-style joiner protocol (#52)

* feat(strip): collapse StripCell into RichText; edge-style joiner protocol

StripCell existed as a parallel cell type to RichText, with two construction
shapes — `(text, style)` and `(parts, style)` — and a "single-style invariant"
that forced the entire cell interior to share one bg, because joiners read
`item.style.bgcolor` to paint transitions between adjacent strip items.

That invariant was [LAW:locality-or-seam] violated in reverse: a
joiner-specific concern (what color the join glyph touches) was pushed up
into the cell type, constraining its interior. The terminal supports
per-column bg natively; the cell type did not, because the joiner protocol
asked the wrong question.

This collapses StripCell into RichText and narrows the joiner protocol to
the question it actually needs:

- StyledRenderable.edgeStyle(side: "left" | "right"): Style — the style of
  the cell-column adjacent to the joiner on the named side. Joiners
  (PowerlineJoiner, CapsuleJoiner, GradientJoiner) read edgeStyle instead
  of `style.bgcolor`. For uniform-styled items both edges return the same
  style; for items with span variation each edge reports the actual
  boundary column.
- RichText implements edgeStyle via span-at-position lookup merged with
  the wrapping base style. RichText already had `spans` for per-character
  styling, `truncate`/`align`/`pad*`/`slice`/`divide` that preserve spans
  through every operation, and `fromFragments` to assemble from a styled-
  template engine output. It was already the cell type we needed; we
  just hadn't been using it as one.
- StripCell + StripCellPart deleted from src and exports.
- RichText.truncate extended with mode: "right" | "left" | "middle" and
  custom marker. Existing `overflow: "ellipsis"` form preserved.

[LAW:one-type-per-behavior] StripCell and RichText had the same behavior
(styled cell-column-sequence with a renderable). Two types → one type.

[LAW:single-enforcer] One truncate/align/pad implementation on RichText.
Consumers no longer need to construct intermediate cells and then mutate
them — the operation is on the cell type directly, lossless by
construction.

Tests updated: strip.test.ts + flexStrip.test.ts + render.test.ts +
text.test.ts (new truncate mode tests). All 1757 tests pass. Bumped to
0.4.0. Docs (docs/strip.md, spec/demos.md) reference StripCell in prose
and will be updated in a follow-up.

* feat(text): public noWrap getter/setter on RichText

Strip cells need to opt out of wrap-to-width when used as Strip items
(otherwise the cell folds internally when the render passes a maxWidth).
`_noWrap` was settable only via the constructor; adding a public accessor
lets consumers configure it after construction — e.g. when assembling a
cell via `fromFragments` and then setting properties.

[LAW:locality-or-seam] The accessor sits alongside the other RichText
field accessors (`end`, `justify`, `overflow`); no new seam, just
exposing an existing private field through the same boundary the type
already uses for its other configurables.

fix(console): make beginCapture/endCapture actually capture (rich-demo-site-pek.6) (#51)

The capture API was dead code: `_buffer: string` used `""` as both the
"not capturing" sentinel and the empty-buffer state, so `_write`'s
`_buffer !== ""` guard could never be true while a capture was active.
`endCapture()` always returned `""`.

[LAW:types-are-the-program] [LAW:enumeration-gap] — replace the
sentinel-string scheme with `_capture: string | null` so the type
itself carries the discriminator. `null` = not capturing; any string
(including `""`) = capturing, this is the buffer. The impossible state
"not capturing, buffer non-empty" is unrepresentable.

[LAW:one-source-of-truth] — adopt redirect semantics (matching Python
Rich's `Console.capture()`): during capture the target receives
nothing. The previous code attempted a tee but was broken in a way
that produced neither outcome.

Tests cover round-trip, redirect (target unaffected), restoration
after endCapture, default-on-misuse, and independent sequential
sessions. 4/5 fail on master, all 5 pass after the fix.

Spec updated to document the redirect semantics.

fix(security): strip OSC terminators from link URLs at the trust boundary (rich-strip-render-d5z.2) (#46)

* fix(security): strip OSC terminators from link URLs at the RichText boundary (rich-strip-render-d5z.2)

A URL containing ESC (\x1b), BEL (\x07), or ST (\x9c) bytes could
prematurely terminate an OSC 8 hyperlink wrap and inject arbitrary
terminal control bytes. The fix sanitizes link URLs at the trust
boundary — RichText — without modifying the Style value type.

- Add Style.withLink(link): structural clone helper, mirrors withoutColor.
- Add sanitizeStyleLink in text.ts as a module-private peer to the
  existing stripControlChars, applied at all four RichText inflow points:
  constructor options.style, the style setter, stylize, append.
- Style stays a faithful container; raw new Style({ link }) does not
  sanitize, so internal callers that already sanitized are not silently
  re-mutated.
- Sanitizer is reference-preserving on clean URLs (no needless clone).

[LAW:single-enforcer] [LAW:locality-or-seam] One sanitizer rule, applied
at the boundary the data crosses. Renderer downstream trusts the
invariant and emits without guards.

7 new tests pin the contract end-to-end: markup/stylize/append/
constructor/setter all strip; raw Style does not; rendered output cannot
escape the OSC 8 wrap.

* fix(security): centralize link sanitization in resolveStyle to close bypass paths

Copilot review on PR #46 identified that the original 4-point wrap
(constructor / style setter / stylize / append) missed three other
style-accepting paths: highlightRegex, highlightWords, and the
per-region span re-resolution in _buildSegments. A caller passing
`new Style({ link: dirty })` to any of those produced a span whose
URL bytes could still escape the OSC 8 wrap downstream.

Fix: move sanitizeStyleLink into `resolveStyle` itself — the single
canonical normalizer for `string | Style | undefined → Style` inside
text.ts. Every current and future RichText method that normalizes
a style argument now inherits sanitization structurally; no
per-callsite wrap to forget.

[LAW:single-enforcer] One enforcement point, applied at the
canonicalization boundary. The 4 explicit `sanitizeStyleLink(...)`
wraps at the original sites become plain `resolveStyle(...)` calls —
the rule lives in one place instead of four. The `style` setter is
the only path that doesn't pass through `resolveStyle` (its argument
is already a Style), and continues to call sanitizeStyleLink
directly so the boundary contract holds for every assignment.

[LAW:locality-or-seam] `_buildSegments`' per-region
`resolveStyle(span.style)` call now provides structural enforcement
at the last render-pipeline step before bytes leave RichText — a
stricter placement than per-entry-method sanitization.

3 new tests pin the previously-bypassed coverage:
- highlightRegex sanitizes
- highlightWords sanitizes
- the Segment emitted by render() carries a sanitized URL end-to-end

* fix(security): wire-byte sanitization at OSC 8 emit + extract shared rule

Copilot round 2 on PR #46 was right: the RichText boundary alone leaves
gaps. A Style with a hostile link can still enter the rendering
pipeline without passing through RichText — `Console.print({ style:
new Style({ link: dirty }) })` routes via Segment.applyStyle and
Style.add (both faithful — preserve link verbatim), so the dirty URL
reaches render.ts and escapes the OSC 8 wrap.

Fix: layered enforcement at two distinct seams, sharing one rule.

- Extract `stripOscTerminators` to `src/core/sanitize.ts` — a leaf
  module that depends on nothing, so render.ts, style.ts, and text.ts
  can all import without inverting the dep graph. [LAW:one-source-of-truth]
  the regex lives in exactly one place.

- text.ts: data-model boundary (unchanged behavior, now imports the
  shared helper). Required by the ticket's acceptance criterion that
  "the stored URL has the ESC/ST stripped" — RichText.spans[].style.link
  is sanitized in-memory so inspection matches what the renderer emits.

- render.ts:segmentsToString and style.ts:Style.render: wire-byte
  boundary. The two OSC 8 byte producers in the codebase now both
  pipe the link through `stripOscTerminators` before interpolation.
  Style itself stays a faithful container — only the bytes going out
  the door are sanitized, the in-memory `style.link` is unchanged.

[LAW:single-enforcer] One rule (the regex in sanitize.ts), applied
at every seam the URL crosses. Forgetting to wrap a future API is no
longer possible — wire bytes are always safe regardless of which
upstream path constructed the Style.

[LAW:locality-or-seam] The two layers are not redundant — they cover
distinct seams: in-memory model cleanness (RichText) vs wire-byte
safety (renderer/Style emit). Together they guarantee dirty bytes
neither live in the data model nor escape on the wire.

Updates the over-claiming comment in text.ts to reflect the layered
enforcement (Copilot was right that the prior text implied a global
invariant the rest of the pipeline didn't enforce).

2 new tests pin the wire-byte boundary: a dirty Style handed straight
to segmentsToString or to Style.render — bypassing RichText, markup,
and every input-sanitizing layer — still produces safe OSC 8 bytes.

* fix(event-router): replace Buffer with Uint8Array + TextEncoder/TextDecoder

EventRouter accepts `Uint8Array | string` from the host but the parser
implementation still relied on node's `Buffer` global — `Buffer.from`,
`Buffer.concat`, `private buffer: Buffer`, `.toString("utf8" | "ascii")`.
A browser host emitting Uint8Array would crash on the missing global
unless the bundler polyfilled Buffer; the type signature was making a
cross-runtime promise the implementation didn't keep.

Refactored to Uint8Array + TextEncoder/TextDecoder end-to-end:
- private buffer: Buffer → private buffer: Uint8Array
- Buffer.from(chunk, "utf8") → UTF8_ENCODER.encode(chunk)
- Buffer.concat([a, b]) → concatBytes(a, b) helper (Uint8Array.set)
- buf.subarray(...).toString("utf8") → UTF8_DECODER.decode(...)

true theorem about the data — the parser actually accepts what the
host promises to emit, instead of widening the type while requiring

pass); browser runtime no longer needs a Buffer polyfill.

the TerminalHost seam — browsers don't expose `setImmediate` and would
require a polyfill for the runtime to load.

semantics match for our use case: deferral until current sync work +
queued microtasks drain so a follow-up chunk in the same tick can
extend a lone ESC into a CSI sequence. The explicit `0` documents that
this is structural deferral, not a throttle — `setImmediate`'s "after
I/O, before timers" distinction is irrelevant when the goal is just
"next macrotask."

[LAW:types-are-the-program] Timer types now honestly represent what's
available in every runtime the seam claims to support, not a node-only
dialect. 8854 tests pass — defer-and-flush behavior is identical.

that it's a pure function of (style, text, colorSystem) — encoding the id

   was added — the doc-comment claimed stability the implementation
   could not honor.

   walk ENTRY_MODULES in package.json#exports order; return the
   exposure from the highest-priority entry the origin appears in
   (alphabetic tie-break only within one entry, for the rare same-
   module rename case). Since ENTRY_MODULES[0] is the primary public
   surface (./ -> src/index.ts), and most multi-exposed symbols are
   surfaced there first, the canonical key cannot shift by adding a
   new exposure to a lower-priority entry. A rename within the
   primary entry DOES shift the key — correct, because that is a
   meaningful change to the public API.

   multi-exposed symbols) all resolve their canonical name to the

* feat: branded CellCol/CodeUnit types; cell-aware TextInput wrap and cursor

Two distinct integer spaces — code-unit index (JS string length/slice) and

plain `number`, allowing silent mixing that breaks on CJK/wide characters.

Introduce CellCol and CodeUnit branded types in cells.ts so the compiler
rejects any mix-up at the call site. Add cellFit() (largest prefix ≤ N cells,
no padding) and cellColToCodeUnitOffset() (single conversion point between
the two spaces). Wrap setCellSize/splitText/chopCells to require CellCol.

Fix all four TextInput bug sites:
- charGreedyWrap: replace Math.min(cap, line.length-pos) with cellFit()
- _renderSingleLine: viewport arithmetic in cell space via splitText
- _emitRowContent: indicator reservation and cursor split via splitText
- _cursorVisualCol / _clampColForRow: return CellCol / accept CellCol → CodeUnit

Update downstream callers (segment.ts, panel.ts, dropdown.ts) with asCellCol()
casts at each call site. Tests extended with wide-char wrap and navigation cases.

* fix: propagate CellCol brand to splitCells, handleMouse, and test call sites

splitCells parameter typed as CellCol — callers in adjustLineLength,
divide, and screen.ts updated with asCellCol() casts. handleMouse converts
click x-offset to code-unit via cellColToCodeUnitOffset, fixing wide-char
click positioning. Stale "No reservation" comment updated to reflect that
_emitRowContent now reserves indicator cells rather than overwriting.
Test charGreedyWrap call sites wrapped with asCellCol so tests participate
in the branded-type safety the PR introduces.

* fix: password-mode click hit-testing and cellColToCodeUnitOffset docstring

handleMouse must map the click's cell offset against the same display
string _renderSingleLine uses — password bullets (1 cell = 1 code unit)
and NEWLINE_GLYPH substitution (also 1:1) — so wide chars in value do
not shift the resulting cursor position. cellColToCodeUnitOffset docstring
corrected: returns the largest code-unit offset whose prefix cell width
≤ cellCol, not "first reaches" (which implied advancing into wide chars).

* fix: surrogate-pair-safe move, delete, and cursor rendering

moveCharLeft/moveCharRight detect low/high surrogates at the cursor
boundary and step 2 code units when the adjacent pair forms an emoji,
so the cursor never lands inside a surrogate pair. Same logic applied
to deleteCharBack and deleteCharForward. _emitRowContent cursor rendering
switches from slice(n, n+1) to String.fromCodePoint(codePointAt(n)) to
extract the full code point without splitting a surrogate pair.

* feat(cells): add CodePoint branded type as third integer space

Cursor positions must never fall inside a surrogate pair. Previously
this was either unguarded or required inline codePointAt/charCodeAt
checks at every mutation site — a [LAW:single-enforcer] violation
scattered across the body.

CodePoint = CodeUnit & { _codePoint } is the compile-time expression
of that invariant. cursorPosition, WrapRow.start, VisualRow.valueStart,
_lineStart()/_lineEnd()/_clampColForRow() all return CodePoint.
nextCodePoint/prevCodePoint are the single authority for stepping across
surrogate boundaries; no caller may advance ±1 code unit directly.

[LAW:types-are-the-program] the illegal state (cursor mid-surrogate) is
now unrepresentable by construction, not guarded at runtime.

* fix(text-input): correct viewport cursor math for wide-char snap; clamp continuation rowPrintWidth

Viewport: splitText snaps backward when startCell falls mid-wide-char,
keeping the whole char in afterStart. cursorDisplayCellCol was subtracted
against the requested startCell rather than the actual start of afterStart.
Fix: actualStartCell = rawCellWidth - cellLen(afterStart), which equals
startCell in the normal case and self-corrects on snap.

Narrow terminal: rowPrintWidth for continuation rows was rawWidth -
markerWidth with no floor; when layout violates the widget's minimum width
the value goes negative, propagating into contentCellWidth arithmetic in
_emitRowContent. Clamped to Math.max(0, ...).

_emitRowContent: contentCellWidth = rowPrintWidth - indicatorWidth was
unguarded; when rowPrintWidth is clamped to 0 (ultra-narrow layout) and an
indicator exists, this goes negative and causes invalid cell-width arithmetic.
Clamped to Math.max(0, ...).

test: WrapRow.start is CodePoint, not ReturnType<typeof asCodeUnit>; asCodeUnit
is no longer imported after the CodePoint refactor.

* fix(text-input/screen): cell-space fallback for Up/Down; brand spliceCells params CellCol

moveLineUp/Down fallback (pre-render): the "ASCII-only" comment hid a real
wide-char bug — col was computed as cursorPosition - lineStart (code-unit
arithmetic), not cellLen of the prefix. Target position was placed with
Math.min(col, lineLen) (also code-unit). Both are now cell-space:
col = cellLen(value.slice(lineStart, cursorPosition));
position = prevLineStart + cellColToCodeUnitOffset(line, clamped col).

screen: lineCellLength return type → CellCol; spliceCells start/length params
→ CellCol; call site wraps x with asCellCol. [LAW:types-are-the-program] —
the cell-column/code-unit distinction is now enforced at the function boundary.

* fix(text-input): snap handleMouse past low surrogate; code-point-aware transposeChars

handleMouse (password mode): "•".repeat(value.length) creates 1 bullet per
code unit, so the resulting code-unit offset can land on a low surrogate
(inside a pair) if value contains emoji. Added low-surrogate check at the
mapped offset — advances 1 CU to the next code-point boundary if needed.

transposeChars: was swapping single code units (value[p-1], value[p]) which
splits surrogate pairs. Rewrote using prevCodePoint/nextCodePoint to extract
full code-point substrings for both char-before and char-at-cursor, then
reassembles. End-of-value path similarly fixed. New cursor = cpAfter, matching

* fix(text-input): code-point-aware word/delete scanning

moveWordLeft, moveWordRight, deleteWordBack, deleteWordForward all walked
by raw UTF-16 code-unit increments (p--/p++) and classified characters via
value[p-1]/value[p] — both wrong for surrogate pairs (emoji, supplementary
chars occupy 2 code units).

Rewrite all four to loop with prevCodePoint/nextCodePoint and classify via
value.slice(prev, p)/value.slice(p, next) so each step moves exactly one
Unicode scalar value and the char fed to isWordChar/isWhitespace is always
a complete code point, never a lone surrogate.

Declare loop variable p: CodePoint (not number) — CodePoint extends CodeUnit
so it's directly assignable to the helpers' CodeUnit parameter without a cast,
and the type expresses the invariant that p never lands mid-surrogate pair.

[LAW:types-are-the-program] the loop variable type now enforces the
code-point-boundary invariant by construction.

* fix: eliminate O(N²) allocation in charGreedyWrap; fix clamp comment

charGreedyWrap called cellFit(line.slice(pos), cap) on every iteration,
materializing the entire remaining tail as a new string each row — O(N²)
total allocation for a line of N characters.

Add cellFitFrom(text, startCU, cap): CodePoint to cells.ts — iterates from
startCU via codePointAt without slicing the tail, returning the end
code-unit offset as CodePoint. Caller slices only the small [pos, end)
chunk for the row content. Loop variable typed CodePoint throughout.

charGreedyWrap rewired to cellFitFrom; force-take path uses nextCodePoint
for the same O(1) boundary advance.

Also corrected the _clampColForRow comment from "one cell before the end"
to "last valid code-point boundary strictly inside the row (which may be
more than one cell before the visual end when the last code point is wide)"
— the implementation was always correct, the comment was misleading.

always stops on a code-point boundary); cellFit semantics unchanged.

* fix(text-input): multiline mouse hit-testing uses row/column coordinates

handleMouse was using single-line coordinate math (subtract 1 for '[' bracket,
ignore event.y, map against the full value string) even in multiline mode.

In multiline mode there are no brackets and each visual row is an independent
content slice. Fix: branch on _multiline.

  - event.y selects the visual row (scrollStart + relY, clamped to rows)
  - continuation rows skip the leading marker cells (markerWidth offset)

A perceptually-uniform color space primitive — the substrate for any
transform that wants equal numerical deltas to mean equal perceptual
deltas (the property HSL famously lacks).

Why this lives here: the manipulation space is a different *behavior*
than the sRGB wire format that terminals consume. Same color, two

hueShift=0); the per-color transform itself runs uniformly for every
var. The branch on isAnchored chooses *which key* to apply, not
*whether* to apply one. [LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow]

guarantees every variant of a semantic root shares the root as its
hyphen prefix, so one set covers the whole family.
[LAW:one-source-of-truth]

* feat(demo): rich-themes-transposed visual fixture

   axis. The error/success/warning swatches stay constant-hue across

   not "the algorithm fails" — it is "the algorithm is honest and a

key-coefficient heuristics or per-operation conventions.

   for `{lightnessScale: -1, lightnessShift: 0}` (crushes everything
   toward L=0 but reported a "flip" to dark=false). The strongest
   theorem is "dark iff background.l < 0.5" — honest under every
   transform. [LAW:types-are-the-program]

The root-hue slider held an absolute target across theme changes, so it never
reflected the newly selected theme. Add a hue-mode toggle:

  relative (new default) — the stored value is an offset from the theme's
    natural tonic hue. 0° = the theme as authored, and the effective hue
    tracks whichever theme is selected, so paging themes shows each untouched.
  absolute — the stored value is the target hue, held across themes, so every
    theme's tonic lands on the same hue ("all in one key").

A single derived `effectiveTargetHue(state)` interprets the mode; the stored
`rootHue` is still preserved across theme changes (orthogonal controls don't

across themes. Absolute mode already displays the actual target hue, which
matches the rendered result.

belonging to the theme. Instead, slide the foreground's OKLCH lightness toward

lightness nearest the original that clears the floor. A blue on a dark-blue
panel becomes a readable lighter blue, not white — the smallest perceptual
change that achieves accessibility, the way professional tone systems do it.

Reuses the same bisection idiom as toRgba's gamut clamp, and lets that clamp
desaturate near the poles so the hue survives and the result stays in-gamut.
Black/white remains only as the degenerate fallback for mid-toned backgrounds
where no lightness of any hue can physically reach the target — there the pole
is also the maximum, matching contrastFor.

the tonic cancelled out: keyFor's hueShift equalled the offset regardless of

change the output advertises a capability that doesn't exist, so remove it
along with TONIC_VARS, tonicIndex, naturalRootHue, and effectiveTargetHue.

no value case. themeKeyForRoot stays in the library as the absolute

terminal output can use them:

  contrastRatio(a, b)          WCAG contrast ratio in [1, 21]

  ensureContrast(fg, bg, min)  make a color readable while keeping its hue,

* fix(widgets,demo): vertical motion no longer parks cursor at wrap boundary

When `moveLineUp` / `moveLineDown` targeted a visual row whose length was
less than the cursor's column, the clamp `min(col, target.length)` landed
cursorPosition at `target.valueStart + target.length` — which equals the
NEXT row's `valueStart` when the target has a continuation row after it
(intra-wrap boundary). `_cursorVisualRow` resolves that boundary toward
the LATER row, so the cursor visibly stayed on the source row even though
its position had moved. Worse, the new position was itself the boundary,
so every subsequent Up/Down recomputed the same clamp and noop'd — cursor
stuck until something independently shifted it (e.g. a no-net-displacement
horizontal jog that left visualCol at 0).

The trace captured the failure end-to-end:

  Up: pos 825 → 812  col=13 → clamp 2 → 812 (= rows[23].valueStart)  ← trap
  Up: pos 812 → 812  (repeated, all noop)
  Right×3 + Left×3 → pos still 812, visualCol=0
  Up: pos 812 → 810  col=0 → clamp 0 → 810  ← works because col=0

Fix: route both vertical motions through `_clampColForRow(col, targetIdx)`,
which clamps to `max(0, target.length - 1)` when the target is followed by
a continuation (intra-wrap), and to `target.length` otherwise (last row of
a wrap, or non-wrapped logical lines — where the next position is the `\n`
separator, not a row-overlap). Cursor now lands strictly inside the target
row, the boundary cannot be reached by vertical motion, and the "state
carryover" symptom disappears.

Also fix the related cosmetic surface in the demo: `templateAtomWrap` was
emitting leading-whitespace as its own visual row (looked empty, since
spaces don't paint visibly against Panel padding). Coalesce a pure-
whitespace leading atom with the following atom in tokenize so the wrap
emits substantive first rows.

A new demo that composes three pickers — category × theme × palette key —

* refactor(widgets): KeyEvent.stop() + priority-tier dispatch chain

KeyEvent becomes a class carrying its own "claimed" signal (event.stop() /
event.stopped) instead of returning a boolean up the call stack. EventRouter
dispatches through an ordered chain — high → focused widget → normal — and
short-circuits on event.stopped. The router holds zero key-specific policy:
Tab/Shift+Tab traversal is owned by FocusManager, which registers itself as
a normal-priority chain participant at construction.

Widgets that consume a key call event.stop(); FocusManager only runs Tab
traversal when no participant upstream stopped it. Dropdown uses this to
suppress traversal while expanded and clears overlay state on blur via a
handleFocus override (single-enforcer for overlay lifecycle).

KeyHandlerOptions added. spec/widgets.md updated to describe the class shape,
FocusManager.handleKey, and the dispatch chain.

priority "high"; rich-config/terminal.ts constructs new KeyEvent instances.

  • mouse_up → focus widget  — router.onMouse

* docs(spec): align widgets.md with implemented API surface

The spec drifted from the contract in src/widgets/types.ts: it documented
`handleClick(MouseEvent)` (the contract is `handleMouse(WidgetMouseEvent)`),
marked widget state fields as `readonly` (they are mutable observables —
the host and widget itself write through actions), and missed the drag
capture mechanism for Slider. Update the spec so a consumer reading it
sees the same contract they'll find in the code.

* test(widgets): drop unused imports; expose StubWidget emit helpers

`emitChange` / `emitSubmit` are `protected` on WidgetBase — calling them
from test code outside the class won't compile under strict TypeScript.
Add public `triggerChange` / `triggerSubmit` wrappers on the local
StubWidget so the subscription tests assert behavior through the
subclass API rather than reaching past the access modifier. Same pass
removes Style + WidgetMouseEvent imports that were no longer referenced
after earlier test refactors.

* fix(template-bindings): error path never throws on invalid errorStyle

renderTemplate promises to degrade gracefully on any failure in the
compile/evaluate/render chain — the catch branch returns a styled
`[error: ...]` segment so live-render callers (preview panes, etc.)
never see an exception. The catch itself was calling Style.parse() on
the caller-supplied `errorStyle` spec, which throws on malformed input,
defeating the whole point of the helper.

Guard the parse with a fallback to a hard-coded safe Style (red dim)
so the helper holds its no-throw contract regardless of what the caller
passes for errorStyle. The default case (no spec) skips parsing
entirely.

* fix(widgets,screen): cursor rewind moves up N-1 rows, not N

After drawing N lines with N-1 separating newlines the cursor sits at
end-of-row-N (no trailing newline). Emitting `\x1b[NA` to rewind moves
the cursor up N rows, landing on the row ABOVE the frame — subsequent
writes then overwrite content the frame doesn't own.

Move the right number of rows: `lastLineCount - 1`. Skip the CSI
entirely when there's only one row to overwrite (some terminals treat
`\x1b[0A` as one row up, which would put us out of bounds the other
direction).

* fix(widgets,slider): reject non-positive / non-integer width at construction

Slider's rendering (`trackChar.repeat(width)`) and mouse math
(`width - 1` denominator) assume `width` is a positive integer.
TypeScript's `number` type can't enforce that, so a caller passing
`0`, `-1`, or `1.5` silently produces corrupt output / NaN values.

Guard once at the construction-time trust boundary so every downstream
call can assume validity. Existing callers passing the default or
sensible explicit widths are unaffected; bad inputs throw a `RangeError`
the caller can attribute back to its own code instead of debugging a
mis-rendered slider.

* fix(widgets,button): clear active state after keyboard activation

Mouse activation pairs naturally (mouse_down sets active, mouse_up
clears it). Keyboard activation had no equivalent clear — pressing
Enter/Space set `active = true` and left it true forever, so the
button kept rendering as visually pressed until something independent
flipped it.

Schedule the clear on the next microtask so the single-frame
`active=true` paint still gives the user the visual "pressed" cue,
then matches the mouse end state. setActive() exists as a public
@action specifically for transitions like this.

* refactor(widgets): single-enforcer hover + reactive theme + cell-aware measurement

Three intertwined widget-framework correctness fixes that live in the
same files, surfaced together by the v0.2 review pass.

Single-enforcer hover (WidgetBase + 5 widgets + InteractiveWidget)
=================================================================
Five widgets each had an identical `@action setHovered`. Lift it to
WidgetBase as the canonical setter and add it to the InteractiveWidget
contract — EventRouter can call `widget.setHovered(inside)` on any
implementor without a function-existence probe or a "synthesize
mouse_move as a fallback" branch. (The router-side cleanup ships in
the next commit, which depends on this one.)

focus()/blur() also route through handleFocus() so subclass overrides
(Dropdown collapses its overlay on blur) see programmatic focus
changes the same way they see event-router transitions. Without this,
calling `dropdown.blur()` flipped `focused` but left the overlay
expanded — a real reachable bug. Test added.

Reactive theme propagation
==========================
`_theme` was a plain class field. setTheme() mutated it, but render()'s
reads weren't tracked by MobX, so Screen's autorun never fired on swap.
Promote to `@observable.ref private accessor _theme` and mark setTheme
`@action` in slider / button / checkbox / toggle / dropdown so theme
changes drive the same re-render path as any other observable state.

Cell-aware widget measurement
=============================
button / checkbox / toggle measure() used `this.label.length`, which
counts UTF-16 code units — wide CJK and emoji labels mis-measure and
break layout. Route through `cellLen` (the cell-width authority used
by core/cells.ts and TextInput). Dropdown's width math
(`maxLabelLen`, `headerText`, padding, clipping) went through
`.length` / `.padEnd` / `.slice`; switch to `cellLen` / `setCellSize`
/ `splitText` so the documented width invariant
(maxLabelLen + 4 cells regardless of filter state) actually holds for
wide/emoji content.

* fix(widgets,event-router): ESC ESC collapse, drag capture, hover via single setHovered

Three input-correctness fixes in the router, plus a parser cleanup:

ESC ESC collapses into one escape event
=======================================
Some terminals double-send the escape key as `\x1b\x1b`. The branch
documented the case but only consumed `bytes: 1`, leaving the second
ESC to flow back through the lone-ESC flush path and emit a second
event — every Esc press triggered handleKey twice. Consume both bytes
so one keypress yields one event.

Drag capture for mouse_move / mouse_up
=======================================
Removing mouse capture broke any widget whose interaction model relies
on dragging outside its bounds (Slider's `_dragging` mode). With pure
topmost-hit dispatch, a mouse_down on the slider followed by mouse_move
into a sibling routed motion to the sibling and orphaned the slider's
drag state; mouse_up on release went wherever the cursor happened to
land, missing the slider's submit altogether.

Restore drag capture: mouse_down records the hit widget; subsequent
mouse_move / mouse_up route to the captured widget unconditionally
until mouse_up clears the capture. Scroll events bypass capture (not
drag-scoped). The branch shape stays data-driven — same pipeline every
event, the captured-widget value picks the target. Tests cover both
the drag-out-and-still-deliver case and the scroll-bypasses-capture
case.

Hover via the canonical setHovered
==================================
Previous fallback path probed `typeof widget.setHovered === "function"`
and otherwise re-dispatched the mouse_move event, which never mutated
`widget.hovered` — so the convergence check `inside !== w.hovered`
re-fired on every move forever. Now that WidgetBase ships a canonical
setHovered (previous commit), the router just calls it. One setter,
no probe, no second code path. The reverse-iter hit-test loop is
extracted to a `topmostHit(widgets, x, y)` helper for readability.

Dead setEncoding block
======================
The start() lifecycle had a `typeof setEncoding === "function"` block
with no body — checked existence but never called it. The buffer
parser handles incomplete UTF-8 by deferring (`consumePrintable`
returns `incomplete` when a multibyte run is truncated), so the
setEncoding hint isn't load-bearing. Drop the dead check.

* fix(widgets,focus-manager): single-dispatch focus transitions

WidgetBase.focus() / blur() now route through handleFocus(), so calling
both widget.blur() AND widget.handleFocus({type:'blur'}) at the manager
level fires every subclass override twice. Idempotent overrides
(Dropdown's clear-filter-and-overlay) survived; non-idempotent
overrides (a custom widget incrementing a focus counter) would not.

Drop the redundant handleFocus calls in unregister / blur / setFocus —
the widget's own focus() / blur() is now the single entry point for the
transition. Test added that pins handleFocus running exactly once per
transition (focus → focus, blur → focus → blur).

* fix(renderables,panel): cell-aware border clipping; document accessory span behavior

Three places in Panel's border rendering clipped with plain
`.slice(0, N)` even though the widths themselves were computed via
cellLen. For wide / emoji characters the byte-count slice cut at the
wrong cell boundary and broke border alignment. Switch all three sites
(title fill, subtitle fill, accessory clip) to `setCellSize` so the
cells written match the cells reserved.

Separately, the BorderAccessory doc claimed "RichText carries its own
styling," but the implementation renders RichText accessories as
`accessory.plain` with the wrapping `accessory.style` applied to the
whole string — per-range spans are dropped. The accessory is meant
for small status indicators (scroll position, count), not arbitrary
span carriers, so update the doc to match: only the wrapping style is
preserved. Codifying the current behavior is more honest than
silently dropping spans; if a future caller needs span-level styling
in a border, that's a separate Panel feature.

* docs(spec): align FocusEvent name, Screen.mount signature, textual-js adapter

Three remaining drift spots vs the implementation:
- `interface FocusEvent` → `WidgetFocusEvent` to match the exported
  type name in src/widgets/types.ts and the rest of the spec.
- Screen.mount documented as `mount(...widgets: InteractiveWidget[])`,
  but the type now accepts MountEntry — a bare widget OR a
  `{ widget, placement }` pair. Document MountEntry / Placement so
  consumers know how to invoke inline / fixed layout.
- textual-js adapter mapping mentioned `widget.handleClick()`; the
  contract is `widget.handleMouse(WidgetMouseEvent)`. Spell out which
  textual-js events map to which mouse types.

* perf(widgets,screen): compute frame once per tick via pendingFrame cache

The autorun called computeFrame() to subscribe to observables it reads;
draw() then called computeFrame() again to actually paint. Every
reactive tick laid out the widget tree twice (render → splitLines →
overlay pass), a real performance hit for non-trivial trees.

Cache the autorun's frame in `pendingFrame` and consume it in draw().
The autorun still subscribes to whatever the render path reads (MobX
tracks reads inside computeFrame either way), so reactivity is
unchanged — we just don't redo the work. draw() falls back to a fresh
compute when invoked outside the autorun (test paths, very first
frame) so behavior survives those cases too.

* fix(widgets): construction-boundary guards for FocusManager + Dropdown

Two trust-boundary issues that produce broken-but-self-consistent state:

FocusManager.register is now idempotent
=======================================
The widget list is a set in spirit. Double-registration would let
next() / prev() cycle through the same widget twice and leave a stale
copy behind after unregister(). Skip when the widget is already
present.

Dropdown clamps selectedIndex to a valid in-range value
=======================================================
Out-of-range `selectedIndex` (or empty options) used to render with
an empty header label and an initial highlightedIndex that pointed
past filteredOptions — the first Enter was a silent no-op. Clamp to
[0, options.length - 1] when there are options; allow empty options
as a legitimate "not populated yet" state with selectedIndex = 0
(render emits an empty label; commit no-ops naturally because
filteredOptions is empty).

Tests added for both guards.

* fix(widgets,static-item): measure via Segment.splitLines

Previous measure walked segments and treated `seg.text === "\\n"` as
the only line break. That ignored embedded newlines inside longer
segment.text — a renderable that emits "a\\nlonger\\nb" as one
Segment was measured as 9 cells when the widest line is 6.

Route through `Segment.splitLines` (the line-break authority used by
the rest of the pipeline) and take the max `Segment.getLineLength`
per line. Adds a test file with three cases covering one-segment-per-
line, embedded newlines, and the options.measure delegate path.

* refactor(widgets,types): drop unused "click" from WidgetMouseEvent.type

EventRouter only ever emits mouse_down / mouse_up / mouse_move /
scroll_up / scroll_down. "click" was never reachable — it was a leftover
from an earlier design where the router might have synthesized clicks.
Keeping unreachable values in the union forces every consumer to handle
a case that never arrives.

Click semantics are derived by handlers (mouse_down + mouse_up on the
same widget). If we ever want a synthesized click event, we add it
deliberately and emit it from the router.

* fix(widgets,event-router): stop() resets per-session parse + drag state

stop() detached the data listener and cleared the ESC timer but left
the parse `buffer` and `capturedWidget` populated. A stop/start cycle
mid-sequence (terminal hand-off, test teardown) leaked half-parsed
bytes into the next session — the first feed after restart could
complete a dangling CSI as a phantom key — and similarly leaked a
held drag capture so the first mouse event after restart routed to
the wrong widget.

Always clear `buffer` and `capturedWidget` in stop() so the router
ends in the same shape a fresh construction would. The cleanup is
also moved outside the `running` guard so repeated stop() (and stop
on a router that was never started) still leaves state empty —
idempotent and defensive.

Tests: two new cases pin "dangling CSI doesn't survive stop" and
"drag capture doesn't survive stop."

* fix(widgets,dropdown): filter caret respects asciiOnly

render() switched the arrow character on `options.asciiOnly`, but the
filter-mode caret in headerText was hard-coded to "│". In ASCII-only
mode the header still emitted the box-drawing character — visible as
mojibake in terminals that can't render U+2502.

Compute the caret in render() (where the option flag lives) and pass
it into headerText as data: "│" normally, "|" under asciiOnly,
"" when not focused. headerText no longer needs to know about the
option flag — same single-enforcer pattern as the arrow.

Test added asserting the ASCII-only render emits "|" and never "│".

* fix(widgets,screen): validate fixed Placement coords at mount

`Placement.kind === "fixed"` accepts `x: number, y: number`, but the
layout pipeline assumes non-negative integers — negative coordinates
indexed out of bounds in paintLines (`lines[y + i]` for y < 0 either
asserts on `!` or skips silently) and fractional coordinates leave the
frame in a wedged shape.

mount() is the trust boundary; validate the placement there and throw
RangeError with the offending coords. The layout pipeline downstream
can then assume validity. Test covers negative x, negative y, and
fractional x.

* fix(widgets,event-router): clear escTimer in stop() regardless of running state

feed() can arm escTimer on a lone-ESC remainder even when the router
was never started (it's a public API). The round-4 stop() reset
guarded escTimer behind the `if (this.running)` block, so a pre-start
feed could leave a deferred escape firing into the next session.

Move escTimer cleanup outside the `running` guard alongside the
buffer / capturedWidget resets (same rationale, same defensiveness).
The full reset is now: clear escTimer, empty buffer, null capture —
unconditionally, every stop().

* docs(spec): clarify onChange/onSubmit are semantic notifications, not render triggers

The InteractiveWidget spec described `onChange` as "host subscribes to
know when to re-render", but the implementation has long since moved
to MobX-driven reactivity for render: WidgetBase.handleFocus,
setDisabled, setHovered, and the various widget hover/active paths
mutate observable state directly without calling emitChange. A host
relying on onChange to drive renders would miss most of them.

Reframe the doc: onChange / onSubmit are app-level semantic signals
(value changed, user activated) — not the render-trigger contract.
Rendering is driven by MobX observable reads in render(); non-MobX
hosts re-render on their own tick / animation-frame schedule.

* test(widgets,integration): pin theme reactivity end-to-end through Screen

Theme reactivity now lives in @observable.ref _theme + @action setTheme
across all five widgets — but the unit tests on widget rendering don't
exercise the Screen autorun, so a regression to a plain field would
have gone undetected at the widget level. (It has broken once already.)

Add a minimal Screen-driven test: mount a Button, capture stdout, swap
its theme, flush microtasks, assert stdout received a new frame. Pinned
end-to-end, not just at the widget surface.

* fix(widgets,event-router): Alt+Space uses canonical "space" key name

Alt-modified decoding routed `ESC <0x20>` through the printable-ASCII
branch, emitting `{ key: " ", character: "", meta: true }`. The
non-Alt path decoded space via the SINGLE_BYTE_KEYS lookup to
`{ key: "space", character: " " }` — so a handler matching
`event.key === "space" && event.meta` would miss Alt+Space.

Consult SINGLE_BYTE_KEYS first on the Alt path too. Alt+Space, Alt+Tab,
Alt+Enter, Alt+Backspace now all get their canonical key names with
`meta: true`. The existing standalone Alt+Backspace branch is folded
into the lookup (0x08 / 0x7f are already in SINGLE_BYTE_KEYS). Test
added pinning Alt+Space → "space".

* test(widgets,screen): pin single-line redraw emits no cursor-up CSI

The redraw path skips the cursor-up CSI when `lastLineCount <= 1`
because some terminals treat `\\x1b[0A` as one row up — a surprise
off-by-one if the frame was a single line. The earlier 2-widget test
covers the N>1 case; this adds the boundary case so a future
"simplification" that always emits `\\x1b[<N-1>A` doesn't silently
regress single-line frames.

* docs(spec): align Button + Dropdown rendering with implementation

Two leftover spec drift spots in the Widgets section:

Button — the spec showed `[ label ]` flatly, but the implementation
emits surrounding spaces when unfocused and switches to brackets only
when focused. The full state composition (disabled > active > hover >
normal) and the active-differentiation-via-bold detail are documented
so the spec matches what render() actually emits.

Dropdown — the spec showed `selected ▾`, but the actual collapsed
shape is `[ <padded-label> ▾ ]` at the documented width invariant
(maxLabelLen + 4). Filter-mode caret and asciiOnly fallbacks are also
described, plus the expanded overlay shape (rows beneath the header,
highlight + selected color pairings) since the spec is meant to be
normative.

* fix(widgets,event-router): dispatchKey walks a snapshot of the chain

A handler that unsubscribes itself (or another handler) during
dispatchKey would splice the live keyChain array under the running
for-of loop, silently skipping the next handler. The chain is meant to
deliver one event to every registered participant (subject to stop());
shifting indices breaks that contract.

Snapshot the chain once at the start of dispatch. Late registrations
join for the next event, late removals take effect after the current
event finishes — same shape as DOM-style listener queues. Both
high-priority and normal-priority passes reuse the same snapshot.

* refactor(widgets,types): use Unsubscribe alias for InteractiveWidget subscriptions

InteractiveWidget.onChange/onSubmit returned the spelled-out
\`() => void\` while every other subscription in this file
(FocusManager.onChange, EventRouter.onKey/onMouse) returns the
\`Unsubscribe\` type alias. Single name for the same idea — easier to
search, harder to drift, and matches the export already defined here.

* test(widgets,event-router): correct the drag-capture-clear test comment

The comment claimed "no mouse_move handler is called because no widget
is captured." That's wrong — dispatchMouse does call target.handleMouse
for mouse_move via hit-test (target = b in this case), and the hover
loop additionally flips b.hovered. The assertion only asks about \`a\`'s
mouse_events (which IS the point — the previously-captured widget must
not still receive events) and was always correct; only the explanatory
comment was misleading.

* docs(widgets,widget-base): bounds writer comment is descriptive, not normative

The comment claimed Screen.draw() is the only writer of \`bounds\`, but
test harnesses and custom layout loops also write it directly — the
field isn't a private-to-Screen invariant, it's a public layout-output
slot any host can populate. Reword to "DefaultScreen usage" so the
rationale (non-observable to avoid reactive surface no one uses) stays
clear without implying an enforced invariant the type doesn't carry.

* docs(widgets): align Button + Slider header comments with render()

Two doc-string drift spots in widget headers:

Button — described active as "color reversal" but render() explicitly
does NOT invert fg/bg. Active and hover share the same accent-on /
on-accent pair; active differentiates with bold. The header now
documents that intentional design choice and the reason (inversion
produces unreadable mostly-accent-on-bg-tinted text for accents whose
contrast partner depends on luminance).

Slider — claimed unfilled uses "surface bg / foreground" but render
only sets color: palette("surface") with no bgcolor. The track sits
transparently against whatever the parent renderable paints
underneath; the comment now matches.

* fix(widgets,screen): clip widget lines to remaining screen width; export overlay protocol

Two layout-correctness fixes:

Defensive clipping in computeFrame
==================================
computeFrame computed shape (and thus bounds) from `widgetLines` BEFORE
clipping, while draw() hard-clipped the final composite line at
screen.width. A widget that emitted more cells than its allotted slot
(rogue widget ignoring maxWidth, or an inline placement overflowing the
screen edge) produced bounds wider than what actually got painted —
breaking hit-testing and the inline rightX that subsequent inline
widgets pack against.

Restructure the layout loop: determine x first from placement, then
clip each widgetLine to \`screen.width - x\` cells, then compute shape +
paint + bounds. The shape now reflects the painted reality, and the
inline rightX that downstream widgets pack against matches the
on-screen geometry. Same clip applied to the overlay pass so overlay
bounds also match what gets painted.

OverlayRenderable + hasOverlay public re-exports
================================================
Both lived in src/widgets/types.ts but weren't re-exported from
src/index.ts, so consumers had to deep-import to use the overlay
protocol — which only works for consumers who can navigate the
package's internal layout. Re-export them at the public surface
alongside the other widget types/helpers.

* fix(widgets,examples): consistent shift+tab character; honest demo focus targets

Shift+Tab character normalization
=================================
decodeCSI's ESC[Z special case emitted \`character: "\t"\` while the
non-shifted Tab path (via SINGLE_BYTE_KEYS lookup) emits \`character:
""\`. Handlers that distinguish via key + shift now see consistent
event shape; `character` reflects what the key would print, which for
Tab is nothing — distinguish via \`key === "tab" && shift\`.

rich-theme-designer: focus targets vs theme targets
===================================================
The preview TextInputs (tiArrows / tiIndices) were in \`allInteractive\`
alongside the dropdowns, so focusableAt(x, y) would return them on
click — but they weren't mounted on the Screen, so FocusManager.focus
rejected them and the click silently did nothing. The sample text
told the user "Hit Tab to focus" reinforcing the illusion.

Split into two lists: \`focusTargets\` (only mounted, focus-managed
widgets) and \`themeTargets\` (everything that resolves palette colors,
including the read-only previews so theme swaps still repaint them).
Sample text reworded to make the preview's read-only status explicit.

* fix(widgets,screen): stop() clears pendingFrame and renderScheduled

stop() disposed the autorun but left \`pendingFrame\` populated with
the last FrameLayout (segments + bounds) and \`renderScheduled\` true if
a microtask was in flight. That retains memory after shutdown and
leaves stale state behind that a subsequent start() would carry into
its first frame.

Clear both in stop() — same idempotent-cleanup pattern as
EventRouter.stop.

* fix(widgets,dropdown): clamp seeded highlightedIndex on every expand

The constructor clamps selectedIndex at construction, but selectedIndex
and options are public @observable fields — external code can write
out-of-range values (and filtering can shift the valid range from
under code that captured an index earlier). Without clamping at every
seed site, an out-of-range selectedIndex propagated into
highlightedIndex on expand, and the first Enter committed
filteredOptions[oor] = undefined as a silent no-op.

Add a private \`clampIndex(n)\` helper that owns "is n a legal option
index" and route both expand paths (keyboard + mouse) through it. Test
added: external write to selectedIndex = 99 with 3 options expand →
highlightedIndex is a legal index.

* fix(test,widgets): restore InteractiveWidget import in focus-manager test

The earlier import cleanup dropped \`InteractiveWidget\` along with the
unused \`WidgetMouseEvent\`, but the test still references it in two
\`changes: (InteractiveWidget | null)[]\` declarations. vitest's esbuild
strips types without checking so the suite still ran, but \`tsc
--noEmit\` would have failed — and \`npm run lint\` only checks src/,
so the gap stayed hidden.

* fix(widgets,screen): capture width once per frame so layout + paint can't drift

\`this.width\` was read in multiple places (renderOptions.maxWidth,
per-widget clipping, per-line clipping at paint time). Between the
autorun's computeFrame and the microtask-scheduled draw, the terminal
can resize — bounds get computed for one width, lines clipped for
another. With the new defensive clipping landing this PR the divergence
became more visible (per-widget bounds clip to width-1, paint clips to
width-2 → off-by-N corruption).

Snapshot \`width\` once at the top of computeFrame and store it on
FrameLayout. draw() destructures it from the frame and uses the same
value for the final line clipping. Layout, bounds, and paint all agree
even if this.width changes mid-frame.

* fix(widgets,screen): make hit-test z-order match paint z-order

Screen's overlay pass painted overlay rows on top of the frame and
expanded the owner's bounds, but EventRouter.topmostHit independently
treated mount-order reverse as z-order. The two orders diverge whenever
a widget mounted AFTER an overlay owner happens to live under the
overlay's region — clicks on overlay rows were silently delivered to
the widget underneath instead of the overlay owner.

The fix lifts the z-order discriminator into data the type carries:
- computeFrame() collects each widget whose overlay produced visible
  rows this frame into an activeOverlays Set, published on FrameLayout.
- draw() copies it onto Screen._activeOverlays.
- The widgets getter partitions widgetList into [base, overlay-active]
  so EventRouter's topmostHit (unchanged) returns the overlay owner.

[LAW:single-enforcer] Screen is now the sole authority on both paint
order and hit-test order; the router consumes the result.

[LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow] No new branches in the hit-tester. The
discriminator (overlay-active or not) lives in the per-frame Set; the
router iterates in reverse and returns the first containing widget,
every event.

unmount() drops the widget from _activeOverlays so a getter call
between unmount and next draw can't return a stale reference. stop()
resets the Set alongside pendingFrame, matching the existing
clean-baseline pattern.

Regression coverage in test/widgets/screen.test.ts: mount-order-only
when no overlays active, overlay-active widget sorted last, collapsing
the overlay returns to mount order, unmount drops the widget from
z-order before the next draw.

* feat(template-bindings): register link function with multi-cell contract (rich-template-bindings-5xd)

Adds the `link` function to richTextFuncs(): `{{ link URL child }}` sets
the wrapper Style's link slot, exactly mirroring `Style.parse("link URL")`.
The implementation is one more entry in the existing factory pattern —
no special-case AST node, no LinkFragment subclass, no second emitter
path. The cell-boundary signal consumers walk is `fragment.style.link`
being truthy.

Why one signal is enough — the engine returns one fragment per top-level
template expression, and Style.add propagates `link` from inner to outer
fragment with right-wins-on-conflict semantics:

- {{ link "u1" "a" }} {{ link "u2" "b" }} → 3 fragments, 2 with link
  set, the literal " " between them as inter-cell joiner.
- {{ link "outer" (link "inner" "x") }} → 1 fragment, link = "outer"
  (outer-wins).
- {{ bold (link "u" "x") }} → 1 fragment, both bold and link set —
  link survives the outer wrapping, so it still qualifies as a cell.
- {{ red "hello" }} → 1 fragment, no link → no cells, all joiner.

feat(themes): PaletteResolver — Textual-style spec language (rich-theming-foundation-lq3.3) (#8)

Resolves spec strings against a Palette into ColorTriplets:

  spec = name ("-darken-" N | "-lighten-" N)? (" " NN "%")?
  name = "auto" | <palette var name>

  "primary"                 → palette["primary"]
  "primary-background"      → palette["primary-background"]    (hyphenated names work)
  "primary-darken-3"        → darken(primary, 3)
  "primary 50%"             → alphaBlend(primary, against, 0.5)
  "auto 33%"                → alphaBlend(contrastFor(against), against, 0.33)
  "primary-darken-3 50%"    → modifier first, then composite

Returns null for: invalid syntax, missing var, or alpha/auto without
required `against`. Pure (no internal state).

The modifier regex is right-anchored — `.+` is greedy — so var names that
themselves contain hyphens (like `primary-background`) parse correctly:
the trailing `-darken-N` / `-lighten-N` segment is treated as the modifier
and everything before it is the var name.

`auto` is modeled as a synthetic var whose lookup returns
`contrastFor(ctx.against)`. The modifier→alpha pipeline downstream is
identical for `auto` and named vars; the only branch is at the lookup
seam.

Foundation complete for layer-1 of the theming redesign per
design-docs/STATUSLINE-THEMING.md. Layers 2 (PaletteMapping) and 3
(cascade) live in claude-powerline.

Adds a parts-array construction shape to `StripCell` so consumers can express
inline foreground / attribute variation under a single cell-level bg without
writing a custom `StyledRenderable`. Real driver: claude-powerline's git
status segment, where `S`/`+3` render green and `-2` renders red, all on the
same blue cell.

  new StripCell(parts, style)       // new — parts: { text, style? }[]

construction — `make it impossible` over `policy + hope`.

the parts data, not in branching.

* fix(rich-dash): keep alt-screen from scrolling on overflow

Live appends a trailing newline after each refresh; in alt-screen mode
that scrolls the saved buffer one row per frame whenever rendered output
fills the terminal. The dashboard's content was 59 lines into a 24-row
viewport, so every frame scrolled and the demo looked like inline output
even though Live had entered the alt buffer.

Two adapters in runtime/clip.ts contain the fix without touching core
Live: InjectMaxHeight pushes terminal-height-minus-one into the root
RenderOptions so Layout's column splits distribute correctly, and
ClipHeight slices each panel body to its allotted rows (reserving 2 for
panel borders). Same code path every frame; variability lives in the
height value.
